mcq.q: According to the course, what is THE main challenge that an online retailer faces once it stops running physical stores?
options: The cost of rent, staff and utilities for its retail outlets
The cost of picking each order and shipping it to each customer
The lack of customer data compared with store retailers
Having to hold far more inventory than a store chain does
mcq.explanation: Going online removes stores but moves the cost into fulfilment: every order must be picked and delivered to each door. Fulfilment plus shipping cost is called THE challenge of online retailing, which is why Topics 4 to 7 focus on cutting picking and last-mile cost.
why_wrong: Online retailers have no stores, so saving rent and staff is an advantage, not the challenge.
Online retailers get MORE data (click-stream, demand data), not less.
Online retailers hold LESS inventory because stock is pooled in a few DCs.

mcq.q: An exam answer lists items as 'advantages of online retailing'. Which item does NOT belong on that list?
options: Flexible fulfilment, because any FC can serve any delivery zone
Easier assortment decisions, because there is only one website
Capturing demand data, not just sales data, from click-streams
Fulfilment by manual labour, since picking is done order by order
mcq.explanation: Fulfilment cost (manual labour, with order-picking as the most costly step) is one of the 5 DISADVANTAGES. The trap is that 'flexible fulfilment' sounds similar but is an advantage. Read the word carefully: fulfilment COST is bad, fulfilment FLEXIBILITY is good.
why_wrong: Flexible fulfilment IS one of the 14 advantages (better service, though higher outbound cost).
This IS an advantage: one website replaces a different product mix for each store.
This IS an advantage: online sellers see what customers browsed, not only what they bought.

mcq.q: A classmate says: 'Online retailers need no inventory at all.' Which statement best corrects this?
options: They hold less inventory because stock is pooled in a few DCs, cutting safety stock
They hold more inventory because they must stock every item that they list online
They hold no inventory because every online order is drop-shipped by the supplier
They hold the same inventory as stores, but they keep it in the customer's region
mcq.explanation: 'Less inventory' is one of the 14 advantages: stock is pooled in a few DCs instead of being spread over many stores, so less safety stock is needed. Online retailers still hold stock for speed, control and service, because drop-shipping is too slow at scale.
why_wrong: Amazon showed the opposite: it listed 1M+ titles but stocked only about 2,000.
This is the trap itself. Drop-shipping is used for some items, but online retailers still hold stock.
Inventory is reduced, not the same, and the gain comes from pooling, not from regional stocking.

mcq.q: An online bookseller notices that many shoppers view Book A and then Book B in the same session, even when they buy neither. Which advantage of online retailing does this show?
options: A better cash conversion cycle due to higher inventory turns
Flexible fulfilment since any FC can ship to any delivery zone
Capturing demand data, not just sales data, from the click-stream
Easier inventory tracking because stock is held in fewer places
mcq.explanation: A store only sees what was bought (sales data). An online retailer also sees what was viewed, searched and put together (click-stream). The course example is exactly this: items A and B viewed together can be shown or bundled together.
why_wrong: The cash cycle is about timing of payments, not about browsing behaviour.
Flexible fulfilment is about which warehouse ships an order, not about customer browsing.
Tracking is about locating stock, not about learning what customers look at.

mcq.q: Amazon is paid by customers 19 days before it pays its suppliers, while a typical book retailer pays suppliers 78 days before customers pay. How many days of cash-cycle advantage does Amazon have over the typical book retailer?
options: 59 days
78 days
97 days
19 days
mcq.explanation: Amazon's cash conversion cycle is −19 days; the typical book retailer's is +78 days. The gap is 78 − (−19) = 97 days. Amazon effectively uses its suppliers' money to fund operations, while the book retailer must finance 78 days of stock.
why_wrong: This subtracts 19 from 78 and ignores that Amazon's cycle is NEGATIVE (−19).
This is only the book retailer's cycle; it ignores Amazon's 19-day head start.
This is only Amazon's cycle; the gap must compare both firms.

mcq.q: Use CCC = days of inventory + days of receivables − days of payables. An online retailer turns its inventory in 20 days, collects from card payments in 1 day and pays suppliers after 40 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
options: −19 days
+19 days
+61 days
−21 days
mcq.explanation: CCC = 20 + 1 − 40 = −19 days. A negative cycle means the retailer collects cash from customers 19 days before it pays suppliers, which is the Amazon pattern in the course. High inventory turns (low inventory days) are what make this possible.
why_wrong: Right size but wrong sign: payables (40) are larger than inventory plus receivables (21), so the cycle is negative.
This adds all three numbers; payables must be SUBTRACTED.
This subtracts receivables instead of adding them: 20 − 1 − 40.

mcq.q: Why is a NEGATIVE cash conversion cycle, like Amazon's −19 days, called 'attractive'?
options: It shows that the retailer is late in paying suppliers and may soon go bankrupt
Customers' cash arrives before suppliers are paid, so suppliers fund the operations
It means the retailer holds more inventory, so it can serve more customers
It means the retailer earns a higher profit margin on each book that it sells
mcq.explanation: Because of high inventory turns (a 'stock-less' model) and quick customer payment, Amazon receives money before it must pay suppliers. This free financing lets it grow without borrowing as much working capital. A store retailer must fund 78 days of stock before customers pay.
why_wrong: Paying on agreed terms after collecting cash is normal; it is a strength, not a sign of distress.
A negative cycle comes from LOW inventory days (high turns), not from more inventory.
The cash cycle is about timing of cash, not margin; Amazon's margin was in fact thin.

mcq.q: An online bookstore decides to add electronics, groceries and furniture to its range. According to the course, which is a hidden COST of this product diversification?
options: Losing the sales-tax advantage it had from locating in a convenient state
Losing its click-stream data because the new products are sold offline
Having to give up flexible fulfilment because FCs can no longer share zones
Different packing equipment and different inventory turns across categories
mcq.explanation: Diversifying products is an advantage, but the course lists its catch: more back-end investment, lower margins, different inventory turns, different packing equipment and more inventory. Amazon's net income fell 47% in 2006 partly as variety and free shipping grew.
why_wrong: Sales tax depends on location, not on how many product categories are sold.
The new products are still sold online, so click-stream data is still collected.
Diversifying products does not remove the ability of any FC to serve any zone.

mcq.q: Prof Lim asks: 'Is technology a fixed cost or a variable cost?' What was the answer given in class, and why?
options: Variable: tech spending never stops; it keeps growing with more suppliers, price updates, tracking and new security threats
Fixed: it is paid once at launch, so the cost per order falls to zero as volume grows
Neither: online retailers can avoid technology cost by listing on a marketplace
Fixed: it rises in exact proportion to the number of parcels shipped
mcq.explanation: Your class note on Topic 1, slide 19 records the answer 'Tech is variable cost'. The slide lists why: an online retailer must keep investing in software to link a growing variety of suppliers, constantly update prices and shipping options, track products and shipments, and buy the latest security. The spending grows with the business, so it is not a one-off fixed investment.
why_wrong: Technology is not paid once; the slide stresses continuous updates and new security.
Even marketplace sellers face tech and fees; and the slide is about the online retailer's own costs.
Rising in exact proportion to parcels is not the reason given, and calling it 'fixed' contradicts the class answer.

mcq.q: Compared with a brick-and-mortar retailer, how does an online retailer cope with seasonal peaks such as Christmas or Cyber Monday?
options: Better: it can ship from any FC, so peaks no longer create any pressure
Better: online demand is smoother because shoppers buy all year round
Worse: it works like make-to-order, so it cannot pre-pack orders ahead
The same: both channels send bulk shipments to stores before the peak
mcq.explanation: Online retailers are MORE exposed to seasonal swings. Each order is picked only after it is placed, like make-to-order, so you cannot pre-pack in quiet periods. A store chain can push stock to shelves weeks ahead and let customers carry it home.
why_wrong: Flexible fulfilment helps service, but each order still has to be picked after it arrives.
Online demand is spiky (Amazon gets 400+ orders per second on Cyber Monday).
Only B&M ships in bulk to stores; online must pick and ship each order separately.

mcq.q: In 1995 Amazon listed over 1 million titles but stocked only about 2,000. How did it supply the rest?
options: Bought them from Barnes & Noble stores at a fixed discount
Drop-shipped or ordered on demand from wholesaler Ingram
Printed every copy on demand in its own Seattle warehouse
Kept them in many regional stores near major population centres
mcq.explanation: Amazon's early model was 'sell all, carry few'. Most titles were drop-shipped or ordered on demand from the wholesaler Ingram. Seattle was chosen partly for being near Ingram, plus IT talent and low tax.
why_wrong: B&N was a competitor; Amazon relied on wholesalers like Ingram.
The case says Amazon used drop-shipping and wholesaler orders, not printing.
Amazon had no stores; its model was 'sell all, carry few'.

mcq.q: When Amazon expanded into many warehouses around 2000, which set of problems did the case report, leading it to close McDonough, Georgia in 2001?
options: Higher store rents, more sales staff and longer checkout queues
Loss of click-stream data and weaker personalised recommendations
Higher sales tax in every state, and a ban on drop-shipping
Split shipments, more inventory from more stocking points, IT coordination
mcq.explanation: More warehouses meant one customer order could be split across sites (more shipments), each site needed its own safety stock (more inventory), and systems had to be coordinated. This shows that back-end logistics is the 'iceberg below the waterline' (Bezos).
why_wrong: Amazon had no stores, so store rent and checkout queues do not apply.
More warehouses do not reduce the data Amazon collects on its website.
These are not the expansion problems listed in the case.

mcq.q: Barnes & Noble had 793 stores and a famous brand, yet BN.com was never profitable. What is the main lesson the course draws from this?
options: A store brand does not carry over online by itself; logistics and IT decide success
Online book retailing cannot make a profit, as shown by both B&N and Amazon
A retailer should always run its website as a separate company to save tax
Holding 600k–750k titles online is the key to beating Amazon on selection
mcq.explanation: B&N's legacy systems were not flexible, its online unit was split off as a separate company (to avoid sales tax), and its inventory turned slowly. The lesson is that success online depends on back-end logistics and IT, not on the brand name. 80% of Amazon's IT spend went on back-office logistics.
why_wrong: Amazon became the profitable leader, so online books can be profitable.
B&N did this, and it failed; it took BN.com back in-house in 2003.
B&N held many titles but still lost; turns were only ~2.3–2.8 vs Amazon's 11–21.

mcq.q: In the in-class question 'Should B&N integrate its online and offline channels?', which point is an OPERATIONAL CHALLENGE rather than an advantage?
options: Ordering in store when a title is out of stock, saving the sale
Buy online, pick up in store, with no last-mile delivery cost
Channel conflict over which channel gets credit for a sale
Pooled inventory and customer data shared across both channels
mcq.explanation: Integration brings advantages (saved sales, BOPIS, pooled stock, shared data, easy returns) but also challenges: systems that cannot see store stock, different picking (single units vs cartons), channel conflict over credit and incentives, tax/legal structure, staff training and consistent prices.
why_wrong: This is an ADVANTAGE of integration: the sale is not lost.
This is an ADVANTAGE: it cuts last-mile cost and brings foot traffic.
This is an ADVANTAGE: pooling reduces stock and improves service.

mcq.q: The case reports that online book returns were only 1–2%, far below brick-and-mortar levels. Which other fact from the case best supports Bezos's view that logistics is 'the iceberg below the waterline'?
options: Amazon chose Seattle mainly because of its large book-reading population
80% of Amazon's IT spending went on back-office logistics
Borders outsourced its website to Amazon and focused only on its stores
B&N set up BN.com as a separate company in order to avoid sales tax
mcq.explanation: The 'iceberg' means customers see only the website, while most of the work and money is hidden in the back end. Amazon spending 80% of its IT budget on back-office logistics shows this directly.
why_wrong: Seattle was chosen for nearness to Ingram, IT talent and low tax, not readers.
This is a fact about Borders, not about where Amazon's hidden effort went.
This is about B&N's tax structure, not about hidden logistics work.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's cash cycle chart for Amazon (2007) is a timeline: a book enters inventory on day 0, the customer pays by card at about day 28–31, and Amazon pays the supplier on day 50. What does this chart show?
options: Amazon pays the supplier about 19 days before the customer pays, so it must borrow to fund its stock
Amazon holds each book for about 50 days before any customer buys it
Amazon collects the customer's cash about 19 days before it pays the supplier, so customers' money funds the business
Amazon's cash cycle is +78 days, the same as a typical book retailer's
mcq.explanation: Cash comes in from the customer at about day 31 and goes out to the supplier at day 50, so Amazon holds the cash for about 19 days first. This is the −19-day cash conversion cycle: high inventory turns plus card payment up front mean customers' money funds the business.
why_wrong: The order is reversed: the customer pays first (about day 31), the supplier later (day 50).
Day 50 is when the supplier is paid, not how long the book sits; the customer pays around day 28–31.
+78 days is the typical book retailer (supplier paid day 90, customer pays day 168), not Amazon.

mcq.q: A bar chart in Prof Lim's Topic 1 slides shows Amazon's fulfilment plus shipping cost as a share of net sales from 2009 to 2021. What does the chart show?
options: The share roughly doubled, from about 16% to about 32% of net sales
The share fell steadily as Amazon grew, from about 32% to about 16%
The share stayed flat at about 5%, because robots offset the rising volume
The share rose only slightly, from about 10% to about 12%
mcq.explanation: The chart shows logistics cost rising from about 15.6% to 32.3% of net sales between 2009 and 2021. This is the course's key point: going online moves cost from stores into picking and delivery, and that cost line keeps climbing as volume and free fast shipping grow.
why_wrong: The direction is wrong: the share rose, it did not fall.
The share was never near 5% and did not stay flat.
The rise was large (about 16% to 32%), not a small 2-point change.

mcq.q: Prof Lim shows a US map with Amazon's fulfilment centres (FCs) plotted over population density. What point does the class note make about this map?
options: FCs are spread evenly by land area so that every state gets one
FCs are built next to suppliers' factories to cut inbound shipping
FCs sit only in states with no sales tax, whatever the population there
How closely FC locations match population density is a fulfilment KPI: closer means faster, cheaper delivery
mcq.explanation: The class note on slide 14 says the correlation between warehouse locations and population density is a fulfilment KPI. FCs follow where customers live, which cuts delivery time and outbound shipping cost. 'Convenient' states (tax) also matter, but population is the driver shown on the map.
why_wrong: The map follows population, not land area; empty states do not get FCs.
The map links FCs to customers (outbound), not to suppliers' factories.
Tax is one reason for choosing a state, but the map's point is population density, not tax alone.

mcq.q: Prof Lim asked in class: 'Amazon carries less inventory than a store chain, but it still holds some. Why? And why run several fulfilment centres instead of one?' Which answer is best?
options: Drop-shipping is faster and cheaper at scale, so own stock is only kept for tax reasons
Own stock gives speed and service control that drop-shipping cannot give at scale; several FCs near customers cut delivery time and outbound shipping and add capacity
Suppliers refuse to drop-ship, and one FC would be too small to pool safety stock
Several FCs reduce total inventory, because every extra stocking point lowers safety stock
mcq.explanation: Drop-shipping is too slow and unreliable at scale, so Amazon keeps its own (pooled) stock to control speed and service. Several FCs close to customers mean faster delivery, lower outbound shipping, more capacity and tax/location benefits.
why_wrong: Drop-shipping is the slow, less reliable option at scale; that is why Amazon holds stock.
Fewer FCs pool safety stock better; the reason for several FCs is speed and shipping cost, not supplier refusal.
More stocking points mean MORE inventory (one reason Amazon closed McDonough in 2001), not less.

mcq.q: Under Fulfilment by Amazon (FBA), who stores the goods and ships them to the customer?
options: Amazon stores, picks, packs and ships, and handles customer service
The seller stores the goods and ships each order after Amazon notifies it
A third-party courier stores the goods and Amazon only takes payment
The customer collects the goods from the seller's own warehouse
mcq.explanation: Under FBA the seller first ships its stock to Amazon. When a customer orders, Amazon picks, packs, delivers and handles service. Under SoA the seller does all of this itself. The marketplace operator prefers FBA.
why_wrong: This describes Sell on Amazon (SoA), not FBA.
Under FBA Amazon itself holds the stock in its warehouses.
Neither SoA nor FBA works this way; delivery is to the customer.

mcq.q: In the Sell on Amazon (SoA) model, what happens right after a customer places an order?
options: Amazon picks the item from its own FC and ships it at once
The seller first sends a batch of stock to Amazon's warehouse
The marketplace notifies the seller, who then ships the order
The customer pays the seller directly, outside the marketplace
mcq.explanation: In SoA the marketplace only handles the order and payment. It notifies the seller, who stores, picks, packs and ships. The marketplace pays the seller minus its commission. Sellers are more independent under SoA and can leave more easily.
why_wrong: That is FBA, where stock is already in Amazon's warehouse.
Sending stock to Amazon first is the FBA flow, not SoA.
Money flows customer → marketplace → (minus commission) → seller in both models.

mcq.q: An online retailer sells 50,000 SKUs itself. Market research shows customers also want 2 million slow-moving niche items, each selling a few units a year. Which reason for running a marketplace does this best match?
options: Testing new products, then taking over the winners and selling them itself
Offering one-stop shopping by outsourcing the long tail to third-party sellers
Using marketplace data to adapt the business model to new trends
Reducing seller fees so that more sellers join from other countries
mcq.explanation: A few products drive most sales while many products have low demand (the long tail). A marketplace lets the retailer offer all of them without owning that stock, so customers get one-stop shopping. The three reasons are: long tail/one-stop shop, test new products, and learn from data.
why_wrong: Testing is about trying new items to find winners, not covering many slow movers.
Data use is a separate reason; the problem here is covering slow movers without stock.
Lower fees are not one of the three reasons to run a marketplace.

mcq.q: A marketplace operator notices that a third-party seller's new smart water bottle is selling very fast. The operator then starts buying and selling the same bottle itself. Which reason for running a marketplace does this show?
options: Outsourcing the long tail of slow movers to other sellers
Protecting its brand by controlling delivery service quality
Avoiding overstock risk through a consignment contract
Testing new products, then selling the winners itself
mcq.explanation: Third-party sellers act as free product tests. When an item proves popular, the operator can stock it and sell it directly. This is also why sellers list 'fierce competition, even from the operator' as a disadvantage.
why_wrong: The bottle is a fast seller, not a slow mover in the long tail.
Brand protection is a reason to prefer FBA, not to copy a winning product.
Consignment is about who owns the stock, not about spotting winners.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an ADVANTAGE for a small seller who joins a big online marketplace?
options: Full control over its prices, with no forced promotions from the platform
Risk control, as the platform handles unpaid bills, fraud and disputes
Strong personal brand and a direct relationship with every customer
No competition from the platform operator in the same product lines
mcq.explanation: The seller's 5 advantages are: tap the marketplace's traffic, use its reputation, risk control (unpaid bills, fraud, disputes), cheaper and quicker start, and easier international access. The other options turn the disadvantages around.
why_wrong: Less control over pricing (forced promotions) is a DISADVANTAGE.
Limited personalisation and a weaker brand link is a DISADVANTAGE.
Fierce competition, even from the operator, is a DISADVANTAGE.

mcq.q: A seller on a marketplace complains: 'The platform made me join its 11.11 sale at 30% off, or my products would be hidden.' Which seller disadvantage is this?
options: Less control over pricing
Rules and regulations
Limited personalisation
Fees such as commission
mcq.explanation: Forced promotions are the course's example of 'less control on pricing'. The 5 seller disadvantages are rules and regulations, fees, limited personalisation, fierce competition (even from the operator), and less control on pricing.
why_wrong: Rules exist, but the specific harm here is being forced to cut prices.
Personalisation is about brand and customer link, not price setting.
No fee is charged here; the seller is pushed into a promotion.

mcq.q: 'Firms that control logistics win.' Which is NOT one of the reasons the course gives for why a marketplace operator prefers to provide fulfilment (FBA)?
options: It owns all the detailed data on demand, behaviour and delivery time
It protects its brand image by controlling the quality of service
Sellers find it harder to leave once their stock sits in its FCs
It saves the operator from having to invest in its own warehouses
mcq.explanation: FBA needs MORE warehouse investment from the operator, not less. The three reasons are: data, brand image (service control), and seller lock-in. Fee income and scale economies in its own warehouses are extra benefits from the discussion.
why_wrong: This IS a reason: the operator sees every order in detail.
This IS a reason: delivery quality reflects on the platform.
This IS a reason: FBA creates lock-in.

mcq.q: A small firm makes large, made-to-order wooden dining tables with a high margin and sells about 10 a month. It already has its own delivery van. Which option suits it better?
options: FBA, because Prime eligibility always outweighs the storage fees
FBA, because Amazon handles bulky custom items more cheaply
Sell on Amazon (SoA), keeping storage and delivery in-house
Neither, because marketplaces do not allow made-to-order goods
mcq.explanation: For the seller, the answer is 'it depends'. SoA suits bulky, slow, high-margin or customised goods and sellers with their own logistics. FBA suits small, fast-moving, standard goods. These tables are bulky, slow and custom, and the firm has a van, so SoA fits.
why_wrong: For bulky, slow, custom items, FBA storage fees and handling usually outweigh the Prime benefit.
FBA works best for small, fast, standard goods, not bulky custom ones.
Marketplaces do allow such goods; SoA lets the seller ship them itself.

mcq.q: Which of these is a pure-play marketplace that holds NO inventory of its own?
options: Taobao
JD
Office Depot
RedMart
mcq.explanation: Pure-play marketplaces such as Taobao, Tmall, eBay and Rakuten only connect buyers and sellers; they own no stock. Retailers such as JD (B2C) and Office Depot (B2B) sell their own inventory.
why_wrong: JD is listed as a B2C retailer that sells its own stock.
Office Depot is a B2B retailer that holds its own stock.
RedMart owns its inventory, warehouse and fleet.

mcq.q: Under a consignment contract with revenue sharing, who owns the inventory until it is sold, and what does the retailer keep per unit sold?
options: The retailer owns it; the retailer keeps (1 − r) × price
The manufacturer owns it; the retailer keeps r × price
The manufacturer owns it; the retailer keeps (1 − r) × price
The retailer owns it; the retailer keeps a fixed fee per unit
mcq.explanation: The manufacturer keeps ownership until a unit sells, so the operator carries no overstock risk. For each unit sold, the retailer keeps r·p and the manufacturer gets (1 − r)·p.
why_wrong: Under consignment the stock stays with the manufacturer, and the retailer's share is r·p.
Ownership is right, but (1 − r)·p is the MANUFACTURER's share.
This is not a consignment contract; the retailer does not buy the stock.

mcq.q: A manufacturer consigns 600 units to an online retailer. The price is $40 and the revenue share is r = 0.15. By the end of the season 500 units are sold and 100 are unsold. How much does the manufacturer receive?
mcq.explanation: The manufacturer gets (1 − r)·p per unit sold = 0.85 × $40 = $34. Times 500 units sold = $17,000. The 100 unsold units earn nothing and stay the manufacturer's stock; this is why consignment removes overstock risk for the retailer.
why_wrong: This is the RETAILER's share: 0.15 × 40 × 500.
This pays on all 600 units; under consignment only SOLD units earn money.
This is total sales revenue (40 × 500) before the retailer takes its share.

mcq.q: In Prof Lim's model, a manufacturer's unit cost is Mᵢ = mᵢ + s·vᵢ. A product has production cost mᵢ = $10 and volume vᵢ = 3 litres, and the retailer charges a storage fee s = $2 per litre. What is the manufacturer's cost per unit?
mcq.explanation: Mᵢ = mᵢ + s·vᵢ = 10 + 2 × 3 = $16. The storage fee is charged per unit of VOLUME, so bulky items pay more. The retailer's cost falls by the same amount: Rᵢ = dᵢ − s·vᵢ, so the total cost cᵢ = Mᵢ + Rᵢ does not change; the fee only moves cost between them.
why_wrong: This ignores the storage fee the manufacturer must pay for the space it uses.
This adds s once instead of s × volume (2 × 3 = 6).
This adds s and v (10 + 2 + 3) instead of multiplying them (2 × 3 = 6).

mcq.q: In the Stackelberg game in Prof Lim's consignment model, which statement is correct?
options: Manufacturers lead by setting p and q; the retailer then picks r and s
The retailer leads by setting r and s; manufacturers then choose p and q
Both sides choose at the same time, so it is solved as a static game
The retailer leads by setting p and q; manufacturers then choose r
mcq.explanation: The retailer (leader) sets the revenue share r and storage fee s first. Each manufacturer (follower) then picks its price pᵢ and quantity qᵢ, subject to the capacity Σqᵢvᵢ ≤ V. The game is solved backwards: first the followers' best response, then the leader's choice.
why_wrong: This reverses the roles; the retailer is the leader.
A Stackelberg game is sequential, not simultaneous.
The retailer sets the contract terms (r, s), not prices and quantities.

mcq.q: A marketplace with limited warehouse space hosts both a diamond seller (small, very valuable) and a diaper seller (bulky, cheap). According to Prof Lim's model, what should the retailer do?
options: Set a storage fee s > 0 so bulky, cheap goods do not crowd out valuable ones
Set s = 0, since a revenue share alone always gives the best result
Charge the storage fee per unit sold instead of per unit of volume
Ban the diaper seller, since cheap goods always lower total profit
mcq.explanation: When manufacturing costs differ a lot, the revenue share alone cannot allocate space well, so the retailer should also charge s > 0 per unit of volume. Bulky, cheap diapers then pay for the space they use, leaving room for high-value items. With similar costs, s = 0 is enough.
why_wrong: s = 0 is enough only when manufacturing costs are SIMILAR, which is not the case here.
The model charges s per unit of VOLUME, which is what makes it work for bulky items.
The model uses a fee to ration space, not a ban.

mcq.q: What does Prof Lim's model find about expanding the retailer's warehouse capacity V?
options: It always hurts manufacturers through fiercer competition
It only benefits the retailer, as the leader of the game
It can benefit both the retailer and the manufacturers
It has no effect, because capacity never binds in the model
mcq.explanation: With more space, more goods can be stocked, so more sales happen and both sides can earn more. This is one of the three key results, together with 's = 0 when costs are similar' and 's > 0 when costs differ a lot'.
why_wrong: This is a listed trap: the model shows expansion can help both.
Manufacturers can gain too, because more of their goods fit in.
Capacity Σqᵢvᵢ ≤ V is a key constraint in the model.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's Sell on Amazon (SoA) diagram shows three flows between customer, marketplace and seller: information (dashed), material (red) and money (dotted). Which flow does NOT pass through the marketplace under SoA?
options: Information flow: the seller receives orders directly from the customer
Financial flow: the customer pays the seller directly
Material flow: the seller ships the product straight to the customer, so the marketplace never sees it
All three flows pass through the marketplace; only FBA bypasses it
mcq.explanation: Under SoA the marketplace notifies the seller of the order (information) and collects payment, paying the seller minus commission (money). But the seller stores and ships the goods itself, so the red material flow goes seller → customer and the marketplace never sees the product.
why_wrong: Orders come through the marketplace, which notifies the seller.
The customer pays the marketplace, which pays the seller minus commission.
It is the other way round: under FBA all three flows pass through the marketplace; under SoA the material flow does not.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's FBA diagram shows the seller shipping stock into Amazon's warehouse before any order arrives. The class note adds that the contract typically lasts about 6 months. Which statement is correct?
options: The seller still owns the stock in Amazon's warehouse until it sells, like consignment; Prof Lim's single-period model is about one such 6-month contract
Amazon buys the stock when it arrives and pays the seller at the end of the 6 months
Ownership passes to Amazon after 6 months if the stock has not sold
The seller owns the stock, but the 6-month contract means the model has many periods
mcq.explanation: Class notes: FBA contracts typically run about 6 months and the seller still owns the inventory, which is similar to consignment. Prof Lim's model is a single-period problem, which matches one such contract.
why_wrong: Amazon does not buy the stock; it charges only when a unit sells.
Unsold units are returned to the seller after a period; Amazon does not take ownership.
The model is single-period; one period ≈ one 6-month contract.

mcq.q: In Prof Lim's long-tail chart, a tall red 'head' on the left drops into a long, low yellow 'tail' to the right. What is on the horizontal axis, and which part does the retailer hand to third-party sellers?
options: Time; the red head of early sales
Price; the yellow tail of cheap items
Products/SKUs ranked by sales; the red head of best sellers
Products/SKUs ranked by sales; the yellow tail of slow movers
mcq.explanation: The class note says the horizontal axis is products (SKUs). The red head is the few best sellers the retailer stocks itself; the long yellow tail is the many slow movers that it outsources to third-party sellers, giving a one-stop shop without owning all the stock.
why_wrong: The axis is products, not time.
The axis is products, not price; the tail is low-demand items, not cheap ones.
The retailer keeps the best sellers (red head) for itself.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's chart plots the retailer's and the manufacturers' expected profits against warehouse capacity V. His handwritten note mentions a 'saturation point'. What does the chart show?
options: Both profits keep rising in a straight line with no limit
Both profits rise as V grows, then level off once more space no longer brings more sales because customers will not buy more
The retailer's profit rises while the manufacturers' profit falls, until saturation
Both profits fall after the saturation point because storage fees rise
mcq.explanation: Expanding capacity is a win-win: with more space Amazon can serve more sellers, so both sides' profits rise. But there is a saturation point where customers will not buy more, so the gains flatten out.
why_wrong: The note on saturation means the gains do not go on forever.
Both sides gain; it is not a trade-off between retailer and makers.
The curves flatten at saturation; they do not turn down.

mcq.q: Which statement about online flash sales is correct?
options: They were pioneered by Zulily in the US in 2001
Assortment changes a few times a year, like stores
Short discounted events create urgency, leading to impulse buying
Prices are cut step by step during each event
mcq.explanation: Flash sales run short (under one week), discounted events whose assortment changes very often. The limited time creates urgency and impulse buying. The model was pioneered by Vente Privée (France, 2001); by 2015 the US market was about $4B, led by Zulily (39%), Gilt (18%) and Rue La La (14%).
why_wrong: The pioneer was Vente Privée in France in 2001; Zulily was the US market leader later.
Flash-sale assortment changes weekly or even daily.
Price is fixed during an event; there are no mid-event markdowns.

mcq.q: At a flash-sale retailer, about 50% of first-exposure styles sell out and about 15% sell less than 25% of their stock. What does this suggest?
options: Many prices may be set too low and some too high, so pricing new styles is the key problem
Prices are about right, because the average sell-through is close to target
Repeat-exposure styles are the main issue, as they earn most of the revenue
The retailer should simply order more stock for every style that it sells
mcq.explanation: Selling out may mean the price was too low (money left on the table); selling under 25% may mean it was too high. Because first-exposure styles bring most revenue and have no sales history, predicting their demand and setting their price is the main challenge.
why_wrong: An average can hide big misses on both sides; half selling out is a warning sign.
FIRST-exposure styles bring most of the revenue, so they are the main challenge.
More stock does not fix poor pricing and would raise leftovers for slow styles.

mcq.q: Which point supports the 'SCIENCE' side, i.e. that analytics CAN help price fashion?
options: Fashion trends are hard to put into numbers
There is little data on competitors' prices
How much a style is worth differs by person
Getting one style's prediction wrong has only a small impact
mcq.explanation: The science side says: e-commerce data is rich (click-stream, traffic), some metrics are clear (price, discount, category), there is a clear success measure (large demand), and a single wrong prediction has small impact because there are thousands of styles. The other three options are art-side arguments.
why_wrong: This is on the ART side: hard-to-quantify trends limit analytics.
This is on the ART side: missing competitor data limits a model.
This is on the ART side: subjective value is hard to model.

mcq.q: When building a demand-prediction model for flash sales, how is 'lost sales' classified?
options: Available data
Missing data
Derived data
Competitor data
mcq.explanation: Lost sales are MISSING: once a style sells out, the retailer never sees the extra customers who wanted it (no stock-out time or traffic data). Discount, number of styles, relative price and weekend/weekday are DERIVED. Price, MSRP, timing, competitor prices and quantity sold are AVAILABLE.
why_wrong: Available data includes price, MSRP, timing and quantity sold, which are recorded.
Derived data (e.g., discount, relative price) is computed from available data; lost sales cannot be.
Lost sales are about the retailer's own unmet demand, not competitors.

mcq.q: A style had 100 units and sold all 100 within the first hour of a 24-hour event. A regression uses 'quantity sold = 100' as its demand for this style. What is the problem?
options: Demand is censored: true demand was likely well above 100, so the model under-states it
None: quantity sold equals demand whenever stock runs out before the event ends
Demand is over-stated, because the first hour always has unusually high traffic
The discount is wrong, because it should be measured from cost and not MSRP
mcq.explanation: A sold-out style hides its true demand: we only see that demand was at least 100. Using 100 as demand under-states demand for best sellers and biases the model. This is the 'censored demand' problem, and why lost sales are called missing data.
why_wrong: When stock runs out, sales are capped by inventory, so sales are less than or equal to demand.
About half of sales come in the first hour anyway; the issue is the cap, not over-statement.
Discount IS measured from MSRP; this has nothing to do with the sell-out problem.

mcq.q: A Flashion style has MSRP $39 and is priced at $9.99. It started with 115 units and sold 77. What are its discount and sell-through?
options: Discount ≈ 26%, sell-through ≈ 67%
Discount ≈ 74%, sell-through ≈ 149%
Discount ≈ 74%, sell-through ≈ 67%
Discount ≈ 290%, sell-through ≈ 67%
mcq.explanation: Discount = (MSRP − Price)/MSRP = (39 − 9.99)/39 = 29.01/39 ≈ 0.744 = 74%. Sell-through = Quantity sold / Starting inventory = 77/115 ≈ 0.670 = 67%.
why_wrong: 26% is Price/MSRP (9.99/39); discount is (MSRP − Price)/MSRP.
149% is 115/77, the inverse; sell-through is sold ÷ starting inventory.
290% divides by price instead of MSRP: (39 − 9.99)/9.99.

mcq.q: In the data-to-price method, what is the job of the REGRESSION step compared with the OPTIMISATION step?
options: Regression picks the price X; optimisation estimates a and b
Regression checks the margin rule; optimisation forecasts demand
Both steps estimate a and b, using two different data sets
Regression estimates a and b in Y = a + bX; optimisation picks the price X
mcq.explanation: Step 1 collects data. Step 2 (regression/ML) learns the demand line Y = a + bX from past styles. Step 3 (optimisation) chooses the price X that maximises revenue X·Y subject to the business constraints.
why_wrong: This reverses the two steps, a listed exam trap.
Constraints belong to optimisation; forecasting belongs to regression.
Only regression estimates the demand line; optimisation uses it.

mcq.q: Demand is estimated as Y = 70.50719 − 0.60658X. Ignoring all constraints, which price maximises revenue R = X·Y?
mcq.explanation: R = aX + bX², so dR/dX = a + 2bX = 0 gives X⁰ = −a/(2b) = 70.50719 / (2 × 0.60658) = 70.50719 / 1.21316 ≈ 58.12, with revenue about 2,048.9. This price is not yet checked against the constraints.
why_wrong: This is a/|b|, the price where demand falls to ZERO, so revenue is zero there.
This divides by 4|b| instead of 2|b|.
This is the margin floor, a constraint, not the unconstrained optimum.

mcq.q: Same demand Y = 70.50719 − 0.60658X. Unit cost is 75. Constraints: X ≤ 134.99 (competitor), margin on cost (X − 75)/75 ≥ 50%, X ≥ 5. What is the optimal price X*?
mcq.explanation: Margin rule: X ≥ 75 × 1.5 = 112.5, so the feasible range is 112.5 ≤ X ≤ 134.99. Revenue peaks at 58.12 and falls after it, so the best feasible price is the LOWEST allowed one: X* = 112.5 (Y ≈ 2.27, R ≈ 255.0). The margin constraint binds; the competitor cap does not.
why_wrong: This is the unconstrained best price; it breaks the margin rule (needs X ≥ 112.5).
The competitor cap is NOT binding; revenue keeps falling as X rises past 58.12.
75 is the unit cost; it gives 0% margin, below the 50% floor.

mcq.q: In the same example (cost 75, cap X ≤ 134.99), suppose the 50% margin is measured on PRICE, (X − 75)/X ≥ 0.5, instead of on cost. What happens?
options: X must be at least 112.5, so the answer stays at X* = 112.5
X must be at least 150, so the new optimal price is X* = 150
X must be at least 150, so no price meets both cap and margin
X must be at least 37.5, so the best price returns to X* = 58.12
mcq.explanation: (X − 75)/X ≥ 0.5 → X − 75 ≥ 0.5X → 0.5X ≥ 75 → X ≥ 150. But X ≤ 134.99, so the problem has no feasible price. This is why the lecture margin (on cost) and Flashion's data margin (on price) must not be mixed up.
why_wrong: 112.5 comes from margin on COST; margin on price gives a stricter floor.
150 breaks the competitor cap of 134.99, so it is not allowed.
37.5 is 75 × 0.5, which mixes up the formula.
mcq.source: slides03 / F1 trap (margin on cost vs on price)

mcq.q: For some styles Flashion uses drop-shipping (shipping method 'D'). What does this mean for Flashion?
options: Flashion buys the stock and ships it from its own warehouse
Flashion drops the price step by step until the style sells out
Unsold units are dropped into a later event at a lower price
The brand ships to the customer, and Flashion does not own the stock
mcq.explanation: Under drop-shipping the designer holds and ships the goods and Flashion earns a commission, acting like a platform. 'Own stock vs drop-ship' is one of the key pricing considerations because it changes who carries the inventory risk.
why_wrong: That is the 'F' mode, where Flashion owns the inventory.
Drop-shipping is about who holds and ships stock, not markdowns.
Re-listing leftovers is a separate practice, not drop-shipping.

mcq.q: Why does a rule-based AI system (e.g., 'if black-and-white patches, then probably a panda') struggle compared with a neural network?
options: Rule-based systems need far more labelled data than neural networks
Hand-written rules break down as the problem grows more complex
Rule-based systems need far more computing power than deep learning
Rule-based systems cannot handle any problem, even very simple ones
mcq.explanation: Rule-based AI relies on humans writing if-then rules. That works for simple problems but fails as complexity grows (many exceptions). Neural networks learn patterns from lots of labelled data ('panda / no panda') using computing power.
why_wrong: It is the NEURAL NETWORK that needs lots of labelled data.
Deep learning is the approach that needs heavy computing power.
Rule-based systems work fine for simple problems.

mcq.q: A firm can either hire a few top AI experts with little data, or average engineers with a huge labelled data set. What does the course suggest, and which saying sums it up?
options: Top experts win, because clever rules beat raw data; 'expertise is the oil'
Both do equally well, because accuracy depends only on computing power
Average engineers with lots of data win; 'AI is the electricity, data is the oil'
Top experts win, because neural networks need very little data to learn
mcq.explanation: Neural networks get smarter as they see more examples, so a large data set matters more than a small team of top experts. This is why data is now treated as a natural resource: 'if AI is the electricity, data is the oil.'
why_wrong: The course says more data beats smarter experts; the slogan is 'data is the oil'.
Computing power matters, but accuracy grows with the amount of data.
Neural networks need LOTS of labelled data.

mcq.q: Flashion fixes a style's price for the whole 24-hour event and does not mark it down during the event. What is the main reason given in the case?
options: Markdowns would teach customers to wait for lower prices
The website cannot change prices once an event has begun
Brands supply over 100 units per style, so stock never runs out
Prices are set by competitors, so Flashion cannot change them
mcq.explanation: If customers learned that prices drop later in an event, they would wait (strategic waiting), which hurts sales and the 'steep discount from the start' promise. About 50% of a style's sales happen in the first hour, so the opening price matters most.
why_wrong: This is not the reason given; it is a strategy choice, not a technical limit.
Brands often give fewer than 100 units, and many styles do sell out.
Flashion sets its own prices; competitor prices are hard to even collect.

mcq.q: In the Flashion case, Kate Wilson (data scientist) wants a pricing model, while Priscilla Johnson says 'pricing is an art'. Which recommendation best fits the course's conclusion?
options: Replace the buyers with the model, since pricing is now fully a science
Combine: the model forecasts and suggests a price, and the buyer adds judgement and signs off
Keep pricing as pure art, since new styles have no sales history at all
Price every style to reach exactly 80% sell-through, as buyers target
mcq.explanation: Prof Lim's view is that pricing is scientific but not free of art. The best answer combines both: the model forecasts demand from past first-exposure styles and suggests a price; the buyer adds judgement (trends) and owns the decision. Sceptics can be won over with a pilot or A/B test.
why_wrong: The course says science is not free of art; feature choice and trends need judgement.
Demand for new styles can be learned from similar past styles' features.
80% sell-through is a proxy; the real goal is revenue or profit.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's flowchart of a flash-sale business runs: procurement → event planning → event sales. What happens to units still unsold when an event ends?
options: They are marked down during the same event until they sell out
They go into a later event, so only the first event is a 'first exposure' for that style
They are always returned to the supplier for a full refund
They are moved to the retailer's physical outlet stores
mcq.explanation: The flowchart shows leftover stock flowing back into a later event. The first time a style appears is its 'first exposure', which earns most revenue and is where the pricing problem sits.
why_wrong: Price is fixed during an event; there are no mid-event markdowns.
The flowchart sends leftovers to a later event, not back to the supplier.
Flash-sale sites are online; the chart shows no outlet stores.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's histogram shows the % of stock sold for first-exposure styles. Suppose a style falls in the left-most bar (less than 25% of its units sold). What does the chart suggest about this style?
options: Its price was probably too low, so revenue was left on the table
Its true demand is hidden because it sold out early
It met the buyers' 80% sell-through target
Its price was probably too high, leaving most units unsold
mcq.explanation: Prof Lim reads the chart both ways: the tall 'sold out' bar suggests prices too LOW, while the bars at 0–25% sold suggest prices too HIGH. A style that sold under a quarter of its stock most likely had a price above what customers would pay.
why_wrong: 'Too low' is the reading for the sold-out bar on the right, not the left-most bar.
Hidden (censored) demand applies to styles that SOLD OUT, not ones that sold under 25%.
Under 25% sold is far below an 80% target.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's R output for lm(demand ~ price) gives intercept 70.50719, price coefficient −0.60658 (marked with three stars) and R² ≈ 0.84. Which reading is correct?
options: Each extra $1 in price loses about 0.61 units of demand, and price alone explains about 84% of the variation in demand
Each extra $1 in price adds about 0.61 units, and the model is correct 84% of the time
The best price is $70.51, and 84% of styles will sell out
Demand falls by 60.7% for each extra $1, and price explains only 16% of the variation
mcq.explanation: The line is Y = 70.50719 − 0.60658X: b is negative, so each $1 rise loses about 0.6 units. R² ≈ 0.84 means price explains about 84% of the variation in demand, and the three stars show the price effect is highly significant.
why_wrong: The coefficient is negative (demand falls), and R² is not a 'percent correct'.
70.51 is the intercept (demand at price 0), not a price; R² says nothing about sell-outs.
The slope is 0.61 units per $1, not 60.7%; R² 0.84 means 84% explained, not 16%.

mcq.q: Prof Lim asks: 'Which AI technology will have the biggest impact in the next 10–20 years, and why?' There is no single right answer. Which approach earns the most marks?
options: List as many AI technologies as possible without choosing one, to show breadth
Pick rule-based AI, since it is simple and easy to explain to managers
Choose one technology, justify it by scale, data and how many people it touches, give a course example, and note one risk and one alternative
Argue that the question cannot be answered because the future is uncertain
mcq.explanation: Marks come from a clear choice, a reason tied to data and computing power ('data is the oil'), a course example (e.g. robots in T6, last mile in T7, Flashion pricing) and a fair risk plus an alternative.
why_wrong: A list with no choice and no reasoning does not answer 'which' and 'why'.
Rule-based AI breaks down as problems get complex; the course stresses data-driven neural networks.
Refusing to choose earns no marks; the question asks for a reasoned view.

mcq.q: Compared with a brick-and-mortar (B&M) retailer's demand, what best describes the demand an online retailer's warehouses must serve?
options: Few orders a day, each for a large quantity, sent in bulk to the retailer's own stores
Many orders a day, each for a small quantity, with flexibility over which warehouse ships
Many orders a day, each for a large quantity, always shipped from one fixed warehouse
Few orders a day, each for a small quantity, shipped only by drop-shipping suppliers
mcq.explanation: Online demand comes as many small orders sent to homes. Any warehouse that holds the stock can serve a customer zone, which is called fulfilment flexibility. B&M demand is the opposite: a few large orders to stores, with no fulfilment flexibility.
why_wrong: This describes B&M demand (replenishing stores), not online demand.
Online orders are small, and online retailers are not tied to one fixed warehouse.
Online demand is many orders, and drop-shipping is only a costly backup option.

mcq.q: A supermarket chain's warehouse in the east runs out of rice. Its stores in the east must wait for the next delivery, even though the west warehouse has plenty of rice. Which feature, typical of online retailers, does this chain lack?
options: Vertical integration: owning its own fleet of cargo jets and delivery vans
Pure pull control: starting work only when a downstream worker asks for it
Fulfilment flexibility: any warehouse holding stock can serve the demand zone
Robust optimisation: planning stock so that demand uncertainty is fully removed
mcq.explanation: In B&M supply chains, if one warehouse is out of stock there is no retrieval from another warehouse. Online retailers have fulfilment flexibility: any fulfilment centre (FC) with stock can ship to the zone. That is exactly what this chain lacks.
why_wrong: Owning transport is the Forbes story; the problem here is being unable to ship from another warehouse.
Pure pull is a bucket-brigade feature (T6), not a supply-chain network feature.
Robust optimisation handles uncertain demand; it does not remove it, and it is not what is missing here.

mcq.q: Which sequence shows the online retailer's supply chain network taught in Topic 4, from start to end?
options: Suppliers → regional warehouses (FCs) → local sortation centres → consumers
Suppliers → local sortation centres → regional warehouses (FCs) → consumers
Regional warehouses (FCs) → suppliers → local sortation centres → consumers
Suppliers → retail stores → regional warehouses (FCs) → consumers
mcq.explanation: Goods flow from suppliers into regional warehouses (fulfilment centres), then to local sortation centres, and then out to consumers in the last mile. Sortation centres sit close to customers, so they come after the FCs.
why_wrong: Sortation centres are local and come after the regional FCs, just before the last mile.
Suppliers are the start of the chain; they ship into the FCs.
Stores are not part of this online network; goods flow from FCs to sortation centres.

mcq.q: The first planning decision is 'when and how much to order from each supplier' (replenishment). Which trade-off does it balance?
options: Outbound shipping cost against customer waiting time
Warehouse capacity against the number of sortation centres
Picker travel time against the number of pick aisles
Fixed ordering cost against inventory holding cost
mcq.explanation: Ordering often saves fixed ordering (setup) cost but builds up stock, which raises holding cost. Ordering rarely does the opposite. Replenishment chooses timing and quantity to balance these two costs.
why_wrong: This is closer to the fulfilment decision (which FC ships, to cut shipping cost); replenishment balances ordering cost against holding cost.
Capacity is a constraint in the model, not the trade-off behind ordering.
That is a warehouse picking issue (T5/T6), not a supply-chain ordering decision.

mcq.q: Two weeks before 11.11, a planner decides how many units of a new phone to keep in the Jurong FC and how many in the Tampines FC, based on forecast demand in each area. Which decision is this?
options: Allocation, a push decision made before demand is known
Fulfilment, a pull decision made after demand is known
Replenishment, a pull decision made after demand is known
Allocation, a pull decision made after demand is known
mcq.explanation: Deciding how much to store in each warehouse is allocation. It is done ahead of demand, based on forecasts, so it is a push (anticipative) decision. The aim is to keep each product close to where it will be demanded.
why_wrong: Fulfilment picks which FC ships a real order; here no orders exist yet.
Replenishment is about ordering from suppliers, and it is push, not pull.
Allocation is right, but it is anticipative (push), not reactive (pull).

mcq.q: A customer in Woodlands places an order. Both the Jurong FC and the Tampines FC hold the item, and the system picks the FC with the lowest shipping cost. Which decision is this, and is it push or pull?
options: Allocation; it is push because it happens before shipping
Replenishment; it is pull because it reacts to a known order
Fulfilment; it is pull because it reacts to a known order
Fulfilment; it is push because it is planned in advance
mcq.explanation: Choosing which warehouse retrieves and ships a customer order is the fulfilment decision. It happens after the order arrives, so it is reactive, which means pull. Its goal is to minimise shipping cost given known demand.
why_wrong: Allocation sets stock levels in each FC ahead of demand; here the order is already known.
Replenishment is ordering from suppliers, not choosing which FC ships to a customer.
Fulfilment is correct, but it is reactive (pull), made after demand is known.

mcq.q: Which of the three aggregate supply-chain decisions are classified as PUSH (anticipative)?
options: Allocation and fulfilment
Replenishment and allocation
Fulfilment only
Replenishment, allocation and fulfilment
mcq.explanation: Replenishment (ordering from suppliers) and allocation (stocking each warehouse) are made before demand is known, so they are push. Fulfilment is made after demand is known, so it is pull. Exam trap: allocation is push, not pull.
why_wrong: Fulfilment is pull (reactive); allocation alone is push.
This reverses the rule: fulfilment is the only pull decision.
Fulfilment waits for actual demand, so it is pull, not push.

mcq.q: Why does Prof Lim's JRAF model decide replenishment, allocation and fulfilment together rather than one at a time?
options: Each decision is made by a different company, so they must sign one shared contract
Joint planning removes all demand uncertainty, so no safety stock is ever needed
Off-the-shelf software can only solve one combined model, not three smaller ones
Fulfilment flexibility links them, so the best stock plan depends on how orders will be shipped
mcq.explanation: Because any FC can serve a zone, how much you allocate to each FC changes which FC will ship each order, and that changes what you should order from suppliers. The decisions depend on each other, so planning them separately leads to higher total cost.
why_wrong: The decisions belong to the same retailer's planning; the reason is interdependence, not contracts.
Joint planning lowers cost but does not remove uncertainty; the robust version exists to handle it.
Software is just the solving tool; it is not why the decisions are linked.

mcq.q: An online retailer starts to let any FC ship to any zone (fulfilment flexibility). Which outcome is most likely?
options: Service level rises and shipping cost always falls, so planning gets easier
Service level falls because orders are split across too many FCs
Nothing changes, because flexibility only matters for B&M retailers
Service level rises, but outbound shipping cost can rise and planning gets harder
mcq.explanation: With flexibility, an order can be filled from another FC when the nearest one is out, so service improves. The cost is that some orders ship from further away, which can raise outbound shipping cost, and allocation and replenishment become harder to plan.
why_wrong: Shipping from a far FC can cost more, and planning gets harder, not easier.
Flexibility lets more orders be filled from stock somewhere, so service goes up.
B&M retailers do not have this flexibility; it is a feature of online retail.

mcq.q: Which cost is NOT part of the JRAF model's objective function?
options: Lost-sales or backorder penalty cost
Production cost (fixed setup plus variable cost)
Holding cost of inventory at the FCs
Fulfilment cost of shipping from FCs to zones
mcq.explanation: JRAF minimises production (fixed setup plus variable), holding, allocation and fulfilment costs. Demand must be met in full, with no backlog or lost sales, so there is no penalty cost for shortages in the objective.
why_wrong: Production cost is one of the four terms in the objective.
Holding cost at the FCs is one of the four terms in the objective.
Fulfilment cost is one of the four terms in the objective.

mcq.q: In the JRAF model, how does the model stay feasible even if the FCs cannot hold enough stock to meet all demand?
options: Unmet demand is backlogged to the next period at no extra cost
Warehouse capacity limits are removed during peak periods
Drop-shipping from the supplier acts as an extra, expensive 'FC J+1'
Customers in far zones are simply dropped from the plan
mcq.explanation: The model adds drop-shipping as one more 'warehouse', called FC J+1. It is costly, so it is used only when needed, but it is always available. This means demand can always be met and the model always has a feasible solution.
why_wrong: The model allows no backlog or lost sales; demand must be fully met each time.
Warehouse capacity is a hard constraint; it is not switched off.
All demand must be met; dropping customers would break the demand constraint.

mcq.q: A JRAF constraint says: inventory at FC j next period = inventory now + units allocated to j − units shipped from j. What type of constraint is this?
options: Supplier production capacity constraint
Flow balance constraint
Fulfilment quantity constraint
Allocation quantity constraint
mcq.explanation: This equation links inventory from one period to the next by adding what comes in (allocated) and subtracting what goes out (shipped). That is the flow balance constraint. The other constraints cover supplier capacity, allocating all received units, warehouse capacity and meeting demand.
why_wrong: Capacity limits how much a supplier can make; it does not track stock over time.
That constraint makes sure each zone's demand is fully met.
That constraint makes sure everything received from suppliers is allocated to FCs.

mcq.q: Topic 4 ends by naming the main bottlenecks of an online retailer's operations that later topics tackle. What are they?
options: Order-picking in the warehouse and last-mile delivery
Supplier selection and contract negotiation
Website design and online payment processing
Receiving at the dock and put-away into storage
mcq.explanation: The course flags order-picking (T6) and last-mile delivery (T7) as the main bottlenecks. Picking is about 55% of warehouse operating cost, and last mile can be up to 28% of total delivery cost, so that is where the savings are.
why_wrong: These are procurement tasks; the course points to picking and last mile as the bottlenecks.
These are front-end issues, not the operational bottlenecks studied in T6 and T7.
These steps matter, but picking (~55% of warehouse cost) and last mile are the big ones.

mcq.q: According to the Forbes (2016) reading, which fact about Alibaba's logistics arm Cainiao is correct?
options: It doubled its fleet of leased cargo jets and shipped 1 billion parcels
It was forecast to handle more parcel volume than FedEx by 2019
It aimed to deliver every order by drone within 30 minutes
It planned a $16B investment covering about 1,800 DCs and 97,000 delivery stations
mcq.explanation: Cainiao, formed by Alibaba and partners, planned to invest $16B in about 1,800 distribution centres and 97,000 delivery stations across 600+ cities. The cargo jets, 1 billion parcels, FedEx forecast and drone goal are all Amazon facts, which are common distractors.
why_wrong: These are Amazon facts, not Cainiao facts.
This forecast was about Amazon, not Cainiao.
The 30-minute drone goal was Amazon's.
mcq.source: Forbes (2016) Amazon & Alibaba bet the future on SCM

mcq.q: What is the main lesson of the Forbes (2016) reading on Amazon and Alibaba?
options: Logistics is best outsourced, so e-retailers should rely fully on FedEx and UPS
Logistics is becoming the key success factor, so big e-retailers integrate vertically into it
Amazon has already overtaken Walmart in sales because of its jets
Drones have already replaced trucks for most deliveries in China
mcq.explanation: Old delivery systems are slow and costly, so Amazon (jets, its own parcels) and Alibaba (Cainiao) invest heavily in logistics. Logistics moves from a side function to the critical success factor, and retailers integrate vertically. The trade-off is huge fixed capital in exchange for control.
why_wrong: The article shows the opposite: retailers are building their own networks.
Walmart's sales were still about 4 times Amazon's at the time.
Drones were a future goal (30-minute delivery), not a current reality.
mcq.source: Forbes (2016) Amazon & Alibaba bet the future on SCM

mcq.q: In Prof Lim's figure, one warehouse is marked red 'out of stock', and red arrows run from other warehouses to the zone it normally serves. What does this figure show?
options: Drop-shipping: the supplier ships straight to the customer
Transshipment: stock is moved between warehouses before demand is known
Backlogging: the zone waits until the red warehouse is restocked
Fulfilment flexibility: any warehouse holding the item can serve the zone, which online retailers have and B&M does not
mcq.explanation: Slide 14 shows fulfilment flexibility: if one warehouse is out, another warehouse that holds stock ships to the zone. It raises service level but can raise outbound shipping cost and links replenishment, allocation and fulfilment together.
why_wrong: The arrows start at other warehouses, not at the supplier.
The arrows go from warehouses to the customer zone, not between warehouses.
The point is that the zone does NOT have to wait; another warehouse serves it.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's network diagram (suppliers → regional warehouses → sortation centres → consumers) has a dotted push-pull boundary. Where does it sit, and what does it divide?
options: At the warehouses: stock is pushed up to them before demand is known (replenish, allocate), then pulled out after orders arrive (fulfil)
At the suppliers: everything after the supplier is pulled by customer orders
At the sortation centres: allocation to sortation centres is the pull decision
At the customer's door: every decision, including fulfilment, is made before demand is known
mcq.explanation: The boundary sits at the warehouses. Replenishment and allocation are anticipative (push), made before demand is known; fulfilment (which FC ships) is reactive (pull), made after demand is realised.
why_wrong: Replenishment and allocation are push decisions, so the boundary is not at the suppliers.
Allocation is to FCs/warehouses and is a PUSH decision.
Fulfilment is made after demand is known, so not everything is push.

mcq.q: On the JRAF model slide, next to the variables x, v, w and y there is a variable δ that can only be 0 or 1. What does it do?
options: It marks whether an order is drop-shipped from 'FC J+1'
It records whether customer demand in a zone was met in full
It is a yes/no switch for placing an order with a supplier, so the fixed setup cost is paid only when δ = 1
It sets the share of each FC's capacity that may be used
mcq.explanation: δ is the order on/off switch: x ≤ x̄·δ, so δ = 0 forces x = 0 (no order) and δ = 1 allows an order up to the cap. The fixed setup cost S·δ in the production cost is paid only when an order is placed.
why_wrong: Drop-shipping is modelled as an extra facility J+1, not by δ.
Demand must always be met in full (a constraint), not tracked by δ.
Warehouse capacity is a separate constraint; δ is not a capacity share.

mcq.q: In the JRAF model, which variable is the FULFILMENT decision, i.e. how much to ship from FC j to customer zone k?
options: x
w
v
y
mcq.explanation: In the JRAF model x = replenishment (order from supplier), v = allocation (supplier to FC), w = fulfilment (FC j to zone k) and y = inventory level.
why_wrong: x is the replenishment quantity ordered from a supplier.
v is the allocation of received stock to each FC.
y is the inventory level held at an FC.

mcq.q: Which warehouse operation accounts for about 55% of warehouse operating expense?
options: Receiving
Put-away
Order-picking
Checking and packing
mcq.explanation: The warehouse flow is receiving → put-away → order-picking → checking and packing → shipping. Order-picking is about 55% of operating expense, which is why Topics 5 and 6 focus on it.
why_wrong: Receiving is one step in the flow, but it is not the biggest cost.
Put-away moves goods into storage; it is not the largest cost share.
Packing matters, but order-picking is the single most costly step.

mcq.q: Within order-picking, which activity takes the most of the picker's time?
options: Travelling between pick locations
Searching for the item on the shelf
Reaching and grabbing the item
Printing and checking the pick list
mcq.explanation: Travel takes the most time in order-picking. That is why the course stresses fast-pick areas, good routing heuristics and goods-to-person robots, which all cut walking.
why_wrong: Searching takes time, but travel is the largest share.
Physical picking of the item is short compared with walking.
Paperwork is a small part of picking time.

mcq.q: A shop sells the same T-shirt in red and in blue. How many stock-keeping units (SKUs) is this?
options: One SKU, because it is the same T-shirt design
One SKU per piece held in stock
Two SKUs only if they sit in different racks
Two SKUs, because each colour is a unique product
mcq.explanation: A SKU is a unique product. The same shirt in two colours counts as two SKUs. A customer can order a pallet, a case or a piece of any SKU.
why_wrong: A SKU is a unique product version; a different colour makes a different SKU.
SKUs count product types, not individual pieces.
Storage location does not decide what a SKU is.

mcq.q: Which storage equipment does the course match with PALLET demand?
options: Pallet flow racks
Single-deep (selective) racks
Bin-shelving
Gravity flow racks
mcq.explanation: Pallets are stored on single-deep (selective) racks and moved by counterbalance lift trucks, turret trucks, AS/RS or conveyors. Pallet flow racks sound like a pallet tool but are for cases.
why_wrong: Trap: pallet flow racks are used for CASE picking, despite the name.
Bin-shelving holds pieces of slow movers.
Gravity flow racks hold pieces of fast movers.

mcq.q: A warehouse wants to fit more pallet racks by making its aisles very narrow (about 5–7 ft). Which handling equipment fits best?
options: Counterbalance lift trucks, which turn the whole truck to face the rack
Turret trucks, whose turret turns 90° to reach the racks
Order-picker trucks, which carry many cases per trip
Kiva robots, which bring shelf pods to the picker
mcq.explanation: Turret trucks work in very narrow aisles (5–7 ft) because only the turret turns 90°, not the whole truck. Counterbalance lift trucks move one pallet at a time but need room to turn.
why_wrong: A counterbalance truck needs wide aisles to turn; it does not suit very narrow aisles.
Order-picker trucks are for case picking, not storing full pallets in narrow aisles.
Kiva handles piece picking with shelf pods, not pallets.

mcq.q: A manager says: 'We sell full pallets to supermarkets, so we should buy pallet flow racks.' What is the best reply?
options: Correct: pallet flow racks are the standard storage for pallet demand
Pallet flow racks are for slow-moving pieces, so they suit long-tail items
Pallet flow racks only work with Boston Dynamics robots doing the restocking
Pallet flow racks are for case picking; full pallets go on single-deep racks
mcq.explanation: Pallet flow racks hold pallets on tilted rollers so workers can pick CASES from the front while restocking from the back. They are used for case demand of high-throughput SKUs. Full-pallet demand uses single-deep racks.
why_wrong: This is the classic trap; the name misleads, but they serve case demand.
Slow-moving pieces go on bin-shelving, not pallet flow racks.
Restocking is done from the back aisle; robots are not required.

mcq.q: Which feature makes pallet flow racks suitable for high-throughput SKUs?
options: Picking and restocking happen from different aisles, so they do not block each other
Picking and restocking happen at the same face, so one worker does both
Robots on top of a cube grid lift the bins out
The rack is very shallow, so many SKUs fit in a small space
mcq.explanation: Pallet flow racks are tilted with rollers. Restockers load from the back aisle and pickers take cases from the front aisle. Because the two jobs do not get in each other's way, the rack suits SKUs with high throughput.
why_wrong: Same-face restocking is the bin-shelving feature, which blocks picking.
This describes AutoStore, not pallet flow racks.
Shallow storage is bin-shelving; pallet flow racks are deep lanes.

mcq.q: Pickers in a case-picking area must travel long distances between picks and collect several cases on each trip. Which handling equipment fits?
options: Turret trucks
Counterbalance lift trucks
Order-picker trucks
AutoStore robots
mcq.explanation: Order-picker trucks carry the picker and let them collect multiple cases per trip over long travel distances. They are listed under case demand, along with AS/RS, conveyors and Boston Dynamics robots.
why_wrong: Turret trucks put away and retrieve full pallets in very narrow aisles.
These carry one pallet at a time, which suits pallet demand.
AutoStore handles pieces stored in small bins, not cases.

mcq.q: Why is bin-shelving a poor choice for a fast-moving piece SKU?
options: It is shallow and is restocked at the pick face, so frequent restocking blocks picking
It is deep and restocked from the back, so items expire before they are picked
It can only hold full pallets, so pieces cannot be picked from it
It needs a turret truck to reach every shelf
mcq.explanation: Bin-shelving is shallow, so it holds little stock and needs frequent restocking. Restocking is done at the same face where people pick, which gets in the way. So bin-shelving suits slow movers (the long tail). Hook: 'Bin = Bad for busy items'.
why_wrong: That describes gravity flow racks, which are actually good for fast movers.
Bin-shelving holds pieces, not pallets.
Bin-shelving is reached by hand; no truck is needed.

mcq.q: An e-grocer has a small number of very popular piece items (e.g. instant noodles sold singly). Which storage fits best?
options: Bin-shelving, restocked from the front at the pick face
Single-deep racks, restocked with counterbalance lift trucks
Gravity flow racks, restocked from the back and often with pick-to-light
Pallet flow racks, picked one case at a time
mcq.explanation: Gravity flow racks are deep and tilted, with one case on the face. They are restocked from the back, so picking is not interrupted, and they give high SKU density. They suit fast-moving pieces and are often used with pick-to-light. Hook: 'Gravity = Go-fast'.
why_wrong: Bin-shelving is for slow movers; restocking would block busy pick faces.
Single-deep racks store pallets, not pieces.
Pallet flow racks serve case demand, not single pieces.

mcq.q: Which handling unit is Boston Dynamics' robot listed under in the equipment selection table?
options: Pallet
Piece
All three units equally
Case
mcq.explanation: Boston Dynamics robots move and stack cases, so they appear under case demand, together with order-picker trucks, AS/RS and conveyors. Kiva and AutoStore are the piece-picking robots.
why_wrong: Pallet handling uses lift trucks, turret trucks, AS/RS and conveyors.
Piece handling robots in the table are Kiva and AutoStore.
It is listed only under case demand.

mcq.q: Which statement about automated storage and retrieval systems (AS/RS) is correct?
options: AS/RS can handle pallets only, never pieces
AS/RS can handle pallets, and a bin version can handle pieces
AS/RS is a type of rack used only for slow-moving pieces
AS/RS is a robot that brings whole shelf pods to the picker
mcq.explanation: AS/RS appears in more than one row of the equipment table: it handles pallets, and in a bin version it handles pieces (it also appears under case). Exam trap: do not tie AS/RS to just one unit.
why_wrong: A bin version of AS/RS is listed for piece demand.
That describes bin-shelving; AS/RS is handling equipment.
That describes Kiva, not AS/RS.

mcq.q: A warehouse installs long conveyors to move cases between areas. What drawback does the course point out?
options: Conveyors can only carry pieces, so cases must be broken down first
Conveyors stop pickers from restocking from the back of racks
Conveyors force every worker to follow a bucket-brigade rule
Conveyors split the warehouse into zones, which can cause workload imbalance
mcq.explanation: Conveyors fix where goods flow, so they divide the warehouse into zones. Work in one zone can pile up while another zone is idle, which creates workload balance problems. Sortation conveyors help for cases but are expensive.
why_wrong: Conveyors carry pallets or cases, so no breakdown is needed.
Restocking from the back is a rack design feature; conveyors do not stop it.
Conveyors do not force any worker-coordination rule.

mcq.q: In Group 1's Week 4 answer, piece demand was judged hardest to fulfil. Which reason was NOT part of that argument?
options: Pieces must always be stored on single-deep pallet racks
Every unit is touched, so cost per unit is highest
Demand is erratic and unpooled across many SKUs
Downstream costs are high: single parcels and returns
mcq.explanation: The group gave five reasons: every unit touched, poor fit for mechanisation, erratic unpooled demand, many SKUs and long travel, and costly downstream steps. Pieces are stored on bin-shelving or gravity flow racks, not single-deep pallet racks, so that option is false and not a reason.
why_wrong: This was reason 1 in the group answer.
Erratic, unpooled demand and SKU growth were part of the argument.
Costly single-parcel delivery and returns were reason 5.

mcq.q: Group 1 refined its Week 4 answer: 'difficulty depends on the order profile divided by the handling unit, not on the channel label.' Which example best supports this?
options: A wholesaler ships pallets of cabbage to a supermarket DC (B2B)
B2B orders are usually full pallets, so every B2B seller has easy fulfilment
Amazon is B2C, yet it faces the hardest piece-picking problem in the industry
A Carousell user sells one used iPhone to another user
mcq.explanation: The refinement says the label (B2B/B2C/C2C) does not decide difficulty; the order profile relative to the handling unit does. Amazon, a 'B2C' firm, ships huge numbers of single pieces, which makes its picking very hard. That is the example the group used.
why_wrong: This is a normal B2B pallet case; it does not show the channel label misleading us.
This ties difficulty to the channel label, which is exactly what the refinement rejects.
This is the default C2C piece case; it does not contrast label with difficulty.

mcq.q: A photo shows rows of shallow shelves holding many small bins of different items. Workers pick and restock from the same front face. Which equipment is this, and what is it for?
options: Bin-shelving: piece picking of slow-moving SKUs
Gravity flow rack: piece picking of fast-moving SKUs
Pallet flow rack: case picking of high-throughput SKUs
Single-deep rack: storing full pallets
mcq.explanation: Bin-shelving is shallow and is picked and restocked from the same face, so restocking interrupts picking. That suits many slow-moving piece SKUs (the long tail), not fast movers.
why_wrong: Gravity flow racks are deep and tilted and restocked from the BACK.
Pallet flow racks are tilted with rollers, hold cases, and restock from another aisle.
Single-deep racks hold whole pallets, not small bins.

mcq.q: A rack has deep, tilted shelves. Only one case of each SKU sits on the pick face, lights show the picker which slot to pick from, and new cases are loaded from the back. Which demand type and SKU speed is it for?
options: Pallet demand, slow movers
