Case demand, slow movers
Piece demand, fast movers
Piece demand, slow movers
mcq.explanation: This is a gravity flow rack: deep and tilted, one case on the face, restocked from the back so picking is never interrupted, often with pick-to-light. Workers pick single pieces from the open case, so it suits fast-moving piece SKUs.
why_wrong: Pallets go on single-deep racks; this rack holds cases that pieces are picked from.
Case picking uses pallet flow racks, and back-restocking is for fast, not slow, movers.
Slow piece movers go on bin-shelving; back-restocking and pick-to-light are for fast movers.

mcq.q: A photo shows an ordinary forklift with a heavy weight at the back that balances the load on its forks. It needs fairly wide aisles. Which equipment is this, and which unit does it move?
options: Order-picker truck; cases
Turret truck; pieces in very narrow aisles
AS/RS crane; bins of pieces
Counterbalance lift truck; pallets
mcq.explanation: A counterbalance lift truck is the standard forklift: a counterweight at the back balances the pallet on the forks. It moves pallets and needs wider aisles than a turret truck.
why_wrong: An order-picker truck lifts the worker on a platform to pick cases.
A turret truck has a head that turns 90° for very narrow (5–7 ft) aisles, and it moves pallets, not pieces.
An AS/RS is an automated rack crane, not a driven forklift.

mcq.q: In Prof Lim's photo of a Kiva (Amazon Robotics) warehouse, small square codes are stuck on the floor in a grid. What are they for?
options: Pickers scan them to confirm each item they pick
The robots scan them to know where they are as they drive around
They mark the pick-to-light slots on gravity flow racks
They show where the AutoStore grid's bins are stacked
mcq.explanation: The class note on slide 48 says QR codes are stuck on the floor and the robots scan them to update their location. Kiva drive units then lift shelf pods and bring them to the picker.
why_wrong: Pickers scan items at the station; the floor codes are for robot navigation.
Pick-to-light is on the racks, not codes on the floor.
AutoStore robots run on rails on top of a grid; this is a Kiva floor.

mcq.q: What is a fast-pick area?
options: A separate building near customers where last-mile drivers collect parcels
A reserve area where bulk stock is kept on single-deep pallet racks
An area where workers drop jobs into a buffer when blocked
A 'warehouse within a warehouse' near shipping, restocked from reserve, to cut response time
mcq.explanation: The fast-pick area is a premier region, usually near shipping, where picking is cheap. It is restocked from the reserve. It shortens response time. Gravity flow racks hold the fast movers and bin-shelving holds the long tail.
why_wrong: That is closer to a sortation centre or hub (T4/T7), not a fast-pick area.
The reserve feeds the fast-pick area; it is not the fast-pick area itself.
That is Group 1's buffer variant of bucket brigades.

mcq.q: Which statement correctly gives the bucket brigade rule?
options: Stay in your fixed zone and pass the job to the next zone when your part is done
Carry your job forward until the downstream colleague takes it over, then walk back and take over your upstream colleague's job
Carry your job to the end of the line, then pass the worker in front to start a new job
Wait at your station until the manager assigns the next job to you
mcq.explanation: Each worker carries a job forward until the next worker downstream takes it over (or the last worker finishes it). Then the worker walks back and takes over from the upstream colleague, or the first worker starts a new job from the buffer. This is a pure pull system.
why_wrong: This is zone picking, which causes imbalance and idle time.
Workers do not pass each other; each job is handed over, not carried to the end by everyone.
Bucket brigades need no manager; the same simple rule guides everyone.

mcq.q: A three-person bucket brigade has speeds v1 = 1, v2 = 3, v3 = 4, ordered slowest to fastest. Work content is 1, spread evenly. Which interval of each job does worker 2 cover once the line balances?
mcq.explanation: Σv = 1 + 3 + 4 = 8. Worker 2 covers [v1/Σv, (v1 + v2)/Σv] = [1/8, 4/8] = [1/8, 1/2]. Worker 1 covers [0, 1/8] and worker 3 covers [1/2, 1].
why_wrong: This splits work equally, ignoring that faster workers cover more.
This uses v2/Σv = 3/8 as the end point instead of (v1 + v2)/Σv.
This starts at v2/Σv; the start should be v1/Σv = 1/8.

mcq.q: A bucket brigade has three workers ordered slowest to fastest with speeds 1.0, 1.5 and 2.5 jobs per hour (work content 1, instant walk-back, no passing). What is the long-run throughput?
options: 1.0 jobs per hour
1.67 jobs per hour
5.0 jobs per hour
2.5 jobs per hour
mcq.explanation: When ordered slowest to fastest, the line balances and throughput TH = v1 + v2 + v3 = 1.0 + 1.5 + 2.5 = 5.0 jobs per hour. This is the maximum possible because every worker is busy all the time.
why_wrong: This is the slowest worker's speed; a balanced brigade is not limited to the slowest.
This is the average speed; throughput is the SUM of speeds.
This is the fastest worker's speed only.

mcq.q: Four workers with speeds 1, 2, 3, 4 form a bucket brigade, ordered slowest to fastest. Which interval does worker 3 (speed 3) repeat?
mcq.explanation: Σv = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Worker 3 covers [(v1 + v2)/Σv, (v1 + v2 + v3)/Σv] = [3/10, 6/10] = [0.3, 0.6]. Check: shares are 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, in proportion to speeds.
why_wrong: This splits work equally into quarters, ignoring speed differences.
This is worker 4's interval: (1+2+3)/10 to 10/10.
This uses the wrong sums; worker 3 starts at (1+2)/10 = 0.3.

mcq.q: Three pickers have speeds: Ann = 3, Ben = 1, Cal = 2. The supervisor sets up a bucket brigade the correct way. Which part of each order does Ann pick once the line balances?
options: The last half, [1/2, 1]
The first half, [0, 1/2]
The middle third, [1/3, 2/3]
The last third, [2/3, 1]
mcq.explanation: Order slowest to fastest: Ben (1), Cal (2), Ann (3). Σv = 6. Ben covers [0, 1/6], Cal covers [1/6, 1/2] and Ann covers [3/6, 6/6] = [1/2, 1]. Throughput is 6.
why_wrong: This keeps the listed order (Ann first); the fastest worker must be last.
Shares follow speeds, not equal thirds, and Ann goes last.
Ann's share is v/Σv = 3/6 = 1/2, not 1/3.

mcq.q: A balanced bucket brigade with speeds 1, 2, 3 (slowest to fastest) is joined by a fourth worker with speed 4, placed at the end. By how much does throughput rise?
options: From 6 to 10, about 40% higher
From 2 to 2.5, about 25% higher
From 6 to 10, about 67% higher
From 3 to 4, about 33% higher
mcq.explanation: Old TH = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. New TH = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The increase is (10 − 6)/6 = 4/6 ≈ 67%. Because the new worker is the fastest, putting them last keeps the slowest-to-fastest order, so the line still balances.
why_wrong: The rise is 4/6, not 4/10; divide by the old throughput.
These are average speeds; throughput is the sum of speeds.
These are the fastest worker's speeds; throughput is not set by one worker.

mcq.q: A team runs a bucket brigade with the FASTEST worker first and the slowest worker last. What does the theory say about this line?
options: It still self-balances, because the rule is the same for every worker
Self-balancing is not guaranteed: hand-offs may not settle and the fast worker gets blocked behind the slow one
Throughput still equals the sum of speeds, only the hand-off points move
Throughput rises, because the fastest worker starts every new job sooner
mcq.explanation: The convergence result needs workers ordered slowest to fastest along the flow. With the fastest first, the fast worker catches up with the slower worker ahead and is blocked (no passing). Hand-off points need not converge to fixed spots, so the line may not self-balance and throughput can fall below Σv.
why_wrong: The same rule is not enough; convergence needs slowest-to-fastest order.
TH = Σv relies on the balanced state, which is not guaranteed here.
A fast upstream worker catches up with the slow worker and waits, so output tends to fall.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five advantages of bucket brigades?
options: It is a pure pull system, so WIP stays under control
It self-balances, so task times need not be measured accurately
Workers carry jobs, so no special material-handling equipment is needed
Workers may pass each other, so fast workers are never held up
mcq.explanation: The five advantages are: pure pull (WIP under control), no special material-handling equipment, self-balancing (no need to measure task times), fits teamwork, and a simple identical rule with no management needed. The model assumes NO passing, so passing is not an advantage.
why_wrong: Pure pull with controlled WIP is advantage 1.
Self-balancing without time studies is advantage 3.
No special equipment is advantage 2.

mcq.q: Group 1's Week 5 variant 1: a blocked worker drops the job in a buffer before a busy section and walks back. When does this help most?
options: When the downstream worker is always slower than the upstream worker
When blocking comes from short, random delays, such as a one-person freezer section
When the firm wants orders to finish in strict sequence
When the firm wants to improve self-balancing
mcq.explanation: The buffer removes blocking time caused by short, random delays. Its costs are weaker self-balancing, more WIP and buffer space, out-of-sequence orders and extra handling. Group 1's verdict was a conditional yes: it helps only when delays are random, not systematic.
why_wrong: If downstream is systematically slower, the buffer just fills up and does not help.
Buffers cause out-of-sequence orders, so this is a cost, not a benefit.
Dropping jobs weakens self-balancing, because hand-offs no longer signal speed.

mcq.q: Group 1's Week 5 variant 2 has workers circle through the line instead of walking back. Why was the group doubtful about it?
options: Walk-back is a small share of time, and circling breaks the slowest-to-fastest order so the line stops self-balancing
Walk-back is the largest waste in the line, so circling removes too much useful rest time
Circling needs a buffer between every pair of workers, which costs too much space
Circling makes every worker move at the same speed, so faster workers waste effort
mcq.explanation: Circling removes empty walk-back (up to +25% in one simulation), but walk-back is only a small part of time. Circling also destroys the slowest-to-fastest order: the fast worker laps and gets blocked, so there is no self-balancing and WIP rises. It only makes sense with a loop or U-shaped layout and easy passing.
why_wrong: Walk-back is small; that is why removing it gains little.
Buffers belong to variant 1, not the circling variant.
Workers keep their own speeds; the problem is that the fast worker laps and is blocked.

mcq.q: How does the S-shape routing heuristic work?
options: The picker goes fully through every aisle, including aisles with no picks
The picker enters and leaves each aisle with picks from the same end
The picker goes fully through every aisle with at least one pick and skips empty aisles
The picker goes in up to the largest gap in each aisle and turns back
mcq.explanation: S-shape is the simplest heuristic: traverse every aisle that has at least one pick from end to end, and skip empty aisles. Exam trap: it skips EMPTY aisles only.
why_wrong: S-shape skips aisles with no picks.
This is the return heuristic.
This is the largest-gap heuristic.
mcq.source: slides06 / Ch 6 / de Koster et al. (2007)

mcq.q: Pick lists in a warehouse usually have only one or two picks per aisle. Which heuristic does the course say beats S-shape in this case, and how does it work?
options: Return: enter every aisle from both ends and meet in the middle
Largest gap: go fully through every aisle with picks
Combined: always traverse each aisle fully, chosen at random
Mid-point: front half picked from the front cross-aisle, back half from the back
mcq.explanation: Mid-point splits each aisle into halves: the front half is reached from the front cross-aisle and the back half from the back cross-aisle. With few picks per aisle, this avoids walking full aisle lengths, so it beats S-shape. Largest gap is more efficient still but harder to implement.
why_wrong: Return enters and leaves each aisle from the same end.
Going fully through every aisle with picks is S-shape.
Combined chooses traverse or return per aisle using dynamic programming.
mcq.source: slides06 / Ch 6 / de Koster et al. (2007)

mcq.q: Which statement about routing slow movers is correct?
options: The combined heuristic picks traverse or return per aisle by dynamic programming; the best heuristic averages ~5% worse than optimal
Routing is a TSP that no computer can solve, so only heuristics are possible
The largest-gap heuristic is easier to implement than mid-point but less efficient
The best heuristic is on average about 25% worse than the optimal route
mcq.explanation: Picking route = Travelling Salesman Problem. It is hard in general, but the aisle layout makes it a special case a computer can solve. In practice people use heuristics. The combined heuristic decides, per aisle, to traverse or return using dynamic programming, and the best heuristic is on average about 5% worse than optimal.
why_wrong: Aisles make it a special case that a computer can solve; heuristics are used in practice.
Largest gap is MORE efficient than mid-point but HARDER to implement.
Petersen (1997) found the best heuristic is about 5% worse, not 25%.

mcq.q: A retailer wants goods-to-person picking with the densest storage possible. Its items are small and light. Which system fits, and what is the main limit?
options: Kiva: robots lift whole shelf pods, giving the densest storage with no limits on item size
AutoStore: robots on a cube grid bring bins, but bins are limited to 600×400 mm and 30 kg
AutoStore: robots lift whole shelf pods to the picker, with no item size limits
Kiva: robots on a cube grid bring bins, with lower capex than AutoStore
mcq.explanation: AutoStore stacks bins in a cube grid with no aisles, so storage is densest, and popular bins rise to the top on their own. Its limit is bin size (600×400 mm, up to 30 kg) and higher capex. Kiva lifts shelf pods, handles more item sizes and is easier to scale with lower capex.
why_wrong: Kiva is more flexible on item size, but AutoStore gives the densest storage.
AutoStore moves bins, not shelf pods, and it has bin size and weight limits.
Kiva moves shelf pods, not bins on a grid.
mcq.source: slides06 / Ch 6 / Kiva vs AutoStore notes

mcq.q: Prof Lim's fast-pick diagram runs: reserve storage → restock → fast-pick area → inexpensive picks. If a manager makes the fast-pick area SMALLER, what is the main trade-off?
options: Travel per pick rises, but restocking from reserve is needed less often
Both travel and restocking fall, so smaller is always better
Travel per pick falls, but the area must be restocked from reserve more often
More SKUs fit in the area, so fewer orders need the reserve
mcq.explanation: A smaller fast-pick area packs items closer, so pickers walk less, but it holds less of each SKU and must be restocked more often. A bigger area holds more and needs less restocking. The best size balances pick savings against restocking work.
why_wrong: That is the effect of making the area BIGGER, not smaller.
Restocking goes up when the area shrinks, so there is a trade-off.
A smaller area holds FEWER SKUs and less stock.

mcq.q: In Prof Lim's zone-picking picture, each worker owns a fixed zone. Orders pile up in front of one worker while the worker downstream stands idle. What is the root cause?
options: A static zone assignment is used in a changing system, so work-in-process builds in front of the slowest worker
Workers walk back too slowly after handing off their jobs
The workers are ordered from fastest to slowest along the line
The fast-pick area is too far from the shipping department
mcq.explanation: Work content varies by order, but fixed zones balance only on average. So WIP builds in front of the slowest worker and the next one waits. Cross-training and then the bucket brigade rule fix this.
why_wrong: Walking back is part of bucket brigades, not fixed zone picking.
Worker order by speed matters for bucket brigades; fixed zones fail whatever the order.
The picture is about workload balance between zones, not the area's location.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's time–work chart for a bucket brigade (workers ordered slowest to fastest) shows the hand-off points moving at first and then settling at fixed spots. What does this show?
options: The line needs a supervisor to set zone boundaries from time studies
The line balances itself: each worker keeps repeating the same stretch of work and no one waits (repetition and efficiency)
The line only balances if all workers have the same speed
Work-in-process builds up at the fixed hand-off points
mcq.explanation: When workers are ordered slowest to fastest, hand-off points converge to fixed spots, so the line self-balances. Prof Lim's note: it is balanced because, in the long run, both the repetition and the efficiency conditions are met.
why_wrong: Self-balancing means no supervisor or time study is needed.
Speeds differ; faster workers simply get larger shares of the work.
Bucket brigades are pure pull, so WIP stays under control.

mcq.q: In Prof Lim's routing figure, the picker enters each aisle that has a pick from the FRONT cross-aisle, walks as far as the last pick in that aisle, then comes back out the same front end. Aisles with no picks are skipped. Which heuristic is this?
options: S-shape
Mid-point
Largest gap
Return
mcq.explanation: The return heuristic enters and leaves each aisle with picks from the same end. S-shape walks right through each aisle; mid-point and largest gap use both the front and back cross-aisles.
why_wrong: S-shape fully traverses each aisle with a pick, coming out the other end.
Mid-point picks the back half of aisles from the back cross-aisle.
Largest gap enters from both ends up to the largest gap.

mcq.q: The last mile can be up to 28% of total delivery cost. In the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) used to plan last-mile routes, where does every route start and end?
options: At the fulfilment centre where orders are picked
At the depot, which is the sortation centre
At the first customer on the route
At the driver's home, as in gig delivery
mcq.explanation: The last mile runs from the sortation centre to the receiver. In the VRP, a fleet of vehicles leaves the depot (the sortation centre), visits every customer once at minimum total cost, and returns to the same depot.
why_wrong: The fulfilment centre is earlier in the chain; the VRP depot is the sortation centre (a common trap).
Routes must start and end at the depot, not at a customer.
Gig drivers may start from home, but the VRP model defines routes from and back to the depot.

mcq.q: What does the VRPTW add to the basic Vehicle Routing Problem?
options: A limit on the number of vehicles in the fleet
A rule that each customer is visited twice
A cost for parking and finding the lift
Delivery time windows chosen by customers
mcq.explanation: VRPTW is the VRP with Time Windows: each customer must be served inside a chosen window (e.g., 2-4 pm). This makes the problem even harder; both VRP and VRPTW are computationally hard, so firms use commercial or open-source software.
why_wrong: A fleet is already part of the basic VRP; the 'TW' means time windows.
Each customer is still visited once.
Parking and lift time is one of the 7 practical challenges, not what VRPTW adds.

mcq.q: On a rainy Friday evening Instacart's model forecasts far more orders than it has shoppers available. Based on the case, what does Instacart do?
options: Raises delivery prices to dampen or shift demand
Opens a temporary warehouse to hold extra stock
Hires full-time employees for the evening
Cancels orders below the $35 minimum
mcq.explanation: Instacart uses machine learning to forecast shopper supply and demand by time, weather, traffic and events. When demand is too high, it raises prices to dampen demand or shift it to other slots (Uber, in contrast, raises prices mainly to pull in more supply).
why_wrong: Instacart owns no warehouses; stores are its inventory.
Instacart shoppers are independent contractors, and hiring staff for one evening is not its model.
The $35 minimum applies to all orders; cancelling orders is not the case's answer to peak demand.

mcq.q: A courier in Singapore finds that many customers in office-worker condos are not home during the day, so parcels need repeat visits. Which of the 5 practical last-mile solutions fits this problem best?
options: Drones
Uberization with part-time students
Pick-up stations such as PopStation lockers
Autonomous delivery vehicles
mcq.explanation: The problem is challenge 4, 'customer not home'. Pick-up stations (PopStation, Ninja Van lockers) let the courier drop many parcels at one point in one visit, and customers collect them when convenient, so no repeat trips are needed.
why_wrong: Drones suit sparse, low-density areas and still need someone to receive the parcel.
More part-time couriers add capacity but do not fix the customer being out.
An autonomous vehicle still finds nobody home; it depends on roads and regulation too.

mcq.q: According to the lecture, in which setting are delivery drones most suitable?
options: Sparse, low-density areas with long gaps between drops
Dense city centres with many high-rise flats
Busy shopping malls with many pickup points
Any area, as long as parcels are heavy
mcq.explanation: Drones suit sparse, low-density areas where drops are far apart and a van would drive a long way for each one. Dense cities have airspace, safety and 'last 50 m' problems such as lifts and doors.
why_wrong: This is the exam trap: drones suit sparse areas, not dense cities.
Malls are dense and busy; pickup points there already work without drones.
Drones carry light parcels; heavy items are a weakness, not a fit.

mcq.q: Why is a meal-delivery platform such as Meituan described as a three-sided market?
options: It serves customers, banks and the government
It links riders, scooter makers and petrol stations
It links customers who order, restaurants that cook and share revenue, and drivers who deliver
It runs three channels: website, app and phone
mcq.explanation: In meal delivery, customers place orders; restaurants post menus, cook and share revenue with the platform; drivers pick up and deliver. The platform sets 'required times', manages the order flow and assigns orders to drivers.
why_wrong: Banks and government are not the three sides in the lecture.
Scooter makers and petrol stations are suppliers, not sides of the market.
Channels are not market sides; the three sides are customers, restaurants and drivers.

mcq.q: Meituan Dianping hires and manages its own scooter riders, while Yelp only shows reviews and ads. In the lecture's terms, Meituan is an example of:
options: The US 'go light' model
The China 'go heavy' model
A pure online retailer with no offline service
A one-sided network platform
mcq.explanation: The US model 'goes light': the platform only provides information and matching (Yelp, Airbnb, Uber). The China model 'goes heavy': it also runs the logistics, as Meituan does with its riders (valued at $30B, about 3 times Yelp).
why_wrong: Go light is the US, information-only model, like Yelp.
Meituan delivers meals offline (an O2O service), so it is not a pure online retailer.
Meituan links customers, restaurants and riders, so it is not one-sided.

mcq.q: A user books a home haircut on an app, and a stylist comes to the flat the next day. Which term from the lecture best describes this?
options: Showrooming
Cross-docking
Wave picking
O2O (online-to-offline)
mcq.explanation: O2O means turning an online action into an offline service. The lecture's examples include meals, parcels, home haircuts, hospital queueing and pet cleaning.
why_wrong: Showrooming is trying a product in a store and buying online (T9).
Cross-docking is moving goods straight from inbound to outbound in a warehouse, as RedMart tried.
Wave picking is picking several orders in one trip inside a warehouse.

mcq.q: Which statement best describes Instacart's business model in the case?
options: It owns dark stores and a fleet of refrigerated vans
It owns no warehouses or trucks; freelance shoppers pick in existing stores and use their own cars
It owns inventory but outsources delivery to couriers
It runs robot-picked distribution centres like Webvan
mcq.explanation: Instacart is asset-light: 'We literally don't have any warehouses; we don't have any trucks.' Shoppers are independent contractors who pick from existing supermarket shelves and drive their own cars, so most cost is variable, not fixed.
why_wrong: That describes an asset-heavy grocer such as RedMart, not Instacart.
Instacart holds no inventory; the stores own the stock.
That was Webvan's model, the one that failed.

mcq.q: Webvan built 350,000 sq ft distribution centres at about $35M each and needed about 120,000 customers within 60 miles. What was the main reason it failed?
options: Not enough customer density to fill its routes and centres
Its robots could not pick fresh food
Its prices were higher than Safeway's
It had no website or online ordering
mcq.explanation: Webvan's huge fixed investment only paid off at near-full capacity, which needed many customers packed close together. Too few households ordered (in Oakland only 6.5% tried it once), so the lack of density, not the lack of total customers, sank it.
why_wrong: The case does not blame robot picking; the problem was fixed cost against too few dense orders.
Price is not the reason the case and lecture give.
Webvan was an online grocer, so it did have online ordering.

mcq.q: Table A (Instacart case), per $100 order: gross margin $26.20, HQ and IT $7.00, distribution centre $3.00, delivery $14.00. What is Webvan's expected net profit per $100?
mcq.explanation: Net profit = 26.20 - 7.00 - 3.00 - 14.00 = $2.20 per $100 order. The supermarket makes 26.20 - 7.00 - 5.00 - 12.20 = $2.00, so Webvan was expected to be only slightly more profitable per dollar.
why_wrong: $2.00 is the supermarket's net profit, not Webvan's.
$5.20 forgets the $3.00 distribution centre cost (26.20 - 7.00 - 14.00).
$16.20 forgets to subtract the delivery cost of $14.00 (26.20 - 7.00 - 3.00).

mcq.q: Using Table A, suppose low customer density pushes Webvan's delivery cost from $14.00 to $16.00 per $100 order (all other lines the same). What is Webvan's new net profit, and how does it compare with the supermarket?
options: $2.20, the same as before
$4.20, still above the supermarket
$0.20, well below the supermarket's $2.00
-$1.80, a loss
mcq.explanation: New net profit = 26.20 - 7.00 - 3.00 - 16.00 = $0.20. The supermarket still makes $2.00. A $2 rise in delivery cost wipes out almost all profit, which shows why Webvan needed dense routes.
why_wrong: Delivery cost rose, so profit cannot stay the same.
$4.20 adds the extra $2 instead of subtracting it.
-$1.80 subtracts the $2 increase twice.

mcq.q: Using Table A, at what delivery cost per $100 order would Webvan's net profit exactly equal the supermarket's $2.00?
mcq.explanation: Set 26.20 - 7.00 - 3.00 - D = 2.00, so D = 16.20 - 2.00 = $14.20. Another way: Webvan saves $5.00 warehouse + $12.20 store = $17.20 and spends $3.00 on its DC, so it can afford 17.20 - 3.00 = $14.20 of delivery. Its margin of safety was only $0.20 per $100.
why_wrong: $12.20 is the supermarket's store cost, not the break-even delivery cost.
$17.20 is the cost Webvan saves (warehouse + store) before paying for its own DC.
$16.20 is the delivery cost at which Webvan makes zero profit, not $2.00.

mcq.q: What did Singapore grocer RedMart learn about its operations, according to the interview with its CEO?
options: Cross-docking and outsourced delivery worked well, so it stayed asset-light
Cross-docking and outsourced delivery failed, so it holds its own inventory and runs its own fleet
It should charge suppliers a listing fee to fund delivery
Drivers should be freelance shoppers, as at Instacart
mcq.explanation: RedMart tried cross-docking (suppliers were unreliable) and outsourced delivery (no-shows, errors); both failed. It now owns inventory, a warehouse and a fleet of 20 vans and 3 trucks. The CEO said delivery is the customer touch point, so 'you need to control the last mile.'
why_wrong: RedMart moved away from cross-docking and outsourcing; it did not keep them.
RedMart does not charge suppliers a listing fee.
That is Instacart's model; RedMart is the opposite (own everything).

mcq.q: In the 'Robots vs Uberization' discussion, which zone is human couriers most likely to keep winning this decade?
options: A dense university campus with simple, repeated routes
A flat suburb with wide roads and drone landing points
A sparse rural area with unmapped tracks and hard last-50-metre access
A single office tower with one lobby drop-off
mcq.explanation: Humans win where routes are complex: unmapped areas, lifts, gates and the 'last 50 m', and they are a flexible variable cost at peaks. Robots and drones win where routes are simple (dense campuses, or sparse areas with simple routes). The best platform orchestrates both (DoorDash Dot + Dashers).
why_wrong: Dense + simple routes is the robot zone.
Simple routes with landing points suit drones or road robots.
One lobby drop-off is a simple route; a robot-to-lobby + locker hybrid fits.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's meal-platform chronicle shows two orders, A and B, each with a required time of 11:30. Order A is delivered at 11:25 and order B at 11:35. Which reading is correct?
options: Both orders are on time, because each is within 10 minutes of 11:30
A is 5 minutes early and B is 5 minutes late; the platform sets the required time and assigns the drivers
A is late and B is early, because B was dispatched after A
Both are late, because the required time counts from when the order was placed
mcq.explanation: 11:25 is before the 11:30 required time (early) and 11:35 is after it (late). In this three-sided market the platform sets the required time, manages the order flow and assigns orders to drivers.
why_wrong: There is no 10-minute grace window; 11:35 is past the required time.
The times are the other way round: A arrives before 11:30, B after.
11:25 is before 11:30, so A is not late.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's note on O2O (online-to-offline) says these platforms focus on '衣食住行' (yi shi zhu xing). What does this cover?
options: Luxury goods, travel, entertainment and finance
Electronics, books, music and games
Search, social media, payment and cloud
Basic daily needs: clothing, food, housing and transport
mcq.explanation: 衣 clothing, 食 food, 住 housing, 行 transport: the basic daily needs. O2O turns online actions into offline services for these needs, such as meals, home services and rides.
why_wrong: These are not the basic needs named by 衣食住行.
These are products, mostly sold as pure e-commerce, not O2O daily needs.
These are tech services, not the four basic needs.

mcq.q: Picture 2 in Prof Lim's '5 solutions' slides shows an autonomous delivery vehicle. Which last-mile challenge does it mainly address, and what limits its use?
options: Staff turnover and inconsistent service; its use depends on roads and regulation
Customers not being home; its use depends on locker space
Long gaps between drops in sparse areas; its use depends on flight range
It removes the last mile entirely; its use depends on store opening hours
mcq.explanation: Autonomous vehicles replace drivers, so they fix staff turnover and give consistent service. The slide notes their use depends on roads and regulation.
why_wrong: 'Customer not home' is fixed by pick-up stations (lockers).
Sparse areas with long gaps are the case for drones.
Removing the last mile is buy-online-pick-up-in-store (BOPIS).

mcq.q: Picture 5 in the '5 solutions' slides shows Grab and foodpanda riders. Which statement best describes this 'Uberization' solution?
options: The platform hires a full-time fleet so that service quality stays the same
Customers collect parcels from lockers, so no rider is needed
Part-timers such as students and retirees deliver, giving flexible capacity at peaks at a variable cost
Robots replace riders on simple routes in dense campuses
mcq.explanation: Uberization uses gig workers (part-timers, students, retirees). Capacity grows and shrinks with demand, so it handles peaks and is a variable, not fixed, cost.
why_wrong: A full-time own fleet is the 'go heavy' opposite of gig work.
Lockers are the pick-up station solution.
Robots in dense, simple zones are a different solution from human gig riders.

mcq.q: Airbnb owns no rooms, Uber owns no cars and Alibaba holds no inventory. Which definition of a platform from the lecture explains this?
options: A firm that makes products and pushes them to customers through a linear chain
A retailer that buys stock and resells it online at a mark-up
A business that enables value-creating interactions between external producers and consumers
A logistics company that delivers goods for other sellers
mcq.explanation: A platform enables value-creating interactions between external producers and consumers; it orchestrates a network instead of owning the assets. Because its marginal cost is near zero, it can scale fast.
why_wrong: That is a 'pipe' (make and push), the opposite of a platform.
Buying and reselling stock is a traditional retailer, not a platform.
A logistics firm owns or runs delivery assets; a platform matches others who own them.

mcq.q: An externality is a change in your welfare caused by other people's actions with no compensation. Which is the lecture's example of a NEGATIVE externality?
options: Traffic congestion when more cars use the road
A friend joining your social network
More reviewers posting on Yelp
More drivers joining Uber in your city
mcq.explanation: Traffic congestion is the lecture's negative example: each extra driver slows everyone else and pays nothing for it. A friend joining your social network is the positive example.
why_wrong: A friend joining is the lecture's positive externality.
More reviewers is a positive same-side effect for users.
More drivers is a positive cross-side effect for riders (shorter waits).

mcq.q: Netflix gets better recommendations as more viewers watch, but viewers do not interact with each other, and Netflix simply reacts to what customers do. How does the lecture classify this?
options: Two-sided network effect with a middle-man taking a cut
Negative same-side effect, like more sellers on eBay
Three-sided market, like meal delivery
One-sided network effect, a one-way relationship
mcq.explanation: In a one-sided network, value rises with the number of same-type users (more users, more hits, more sales). The lecture uses Netflix: the platform is reactive to its customers in a one-way relationship.
why_wrong: Two-sided means two groups each gain from the other's growth (e.g., Uber riders and drivers).
More users helps Netflix's recommendations, so it is not a negative effect.
Netflix does not link three separate groups.

mcq.q: A seller on eBay notices that more sellers of the same item have joined, and her sales have dropped. This is an example of:
options: A positive cross-side effect
A negative same-side effect
A positive same-side effect
A negative cross-side effect
mcq.explanation: Same-side effects come from users of the same type (seller to seller). Here more sellers means more competition, so the effect is negative. Same-side effects can be positive (more reviewers) or negative (more competing sellers).
why_wrong: Cross-side means a different group (buyers) affects sellers, which is not the case here.
The seller is worse off, so the effect is negative, not positive.
The effect comes from the same group (sellers), so it is same-side, not cross-side.

mcq.q: A good has NO network effect. Consumer x (0 <= x <= 1) has reservation price r(x) = 1 - x, and the market price is p* = 0.16. What is the equilibrium fraction of buyers x*?
options: 0 only
mcq.explanation: Without network effects, consumer x buys if r(x) >= p, so the equilibrium solves r(x*) = p*: 1 - x* = 0.16, giving x* = 0.84. There is only one equilibrium, and a lower price simply moves x* to the right.
why_wrong: 0.16 is the price, not the fraction who buy.
0.20 and 0.80 are the network-effect equilibria z(1 - z) = 0.16, a different model.
z = 0 as an extra equilibrium only appears with network effects, where f(0) = 0.

mcq.q: With a network effect, consumer x will pay r(x)f(z), where z is the fraction of people using the good. Why is z = 0 ALWAYS an equilibrium?
options: Because r(0) = 0 for the first consumer
Because the curve z(1 - z) peaks at z = 1/2
Because the price is always below 1/4
Because f(0) = 0: if nobody uses the good, it is worth nothing to anyone
mcq.explanation: f(0) = 0, so if everyone expects no one to buy, every consumer values the good at r(x) x 0 = 0, which is below any positive price. No one buys, so the expectation is self-fulfilling and z = 0 is an equilibrium.
why_wrong: With r(x) = 1 - x, r(0) = 1, the highest value, not 0.
The peak at 1/2 decides whether other equilibria exist, not why 0 is one.
Even when p > 1/4, z = 0 is still an equilibrium; it does not depend on the price.

mcq.q: With r(x) = 1 - x and f(z) = z, equilibria satisfy p* = z(1 - z). If p* = 0.16, what are ALL the equilibria?
options: z = 0.2 and 0.8 only
z = 0.84 only
mcq.explanation: Solve z^2 - z + 0.16 = 0: z = [1 +/- sqrt(1 - 0.64)]/2 = (1 +/- 0.6)/2, so z = 0.2 or 0.8. Add z = 0, which is always an equilibrium because f(0) = 0. So there are three: 0, 0.2 and 0.8.
why_wrong: Forgets that z = 0 is always an equilibrium.
0.84 is the answer for the model with NO network effect.
Uses 1 - p and p instead of solving the quadratic.

mcq.q: Same model (p* = z(1 - z)). A platform charges p* = 0.21. What is the tipping point (critical mass) z'?
mcq.explanation: z = [1 +/- sqrt(1 - 4 x 0.21)]/2 = [1 +/- sqrt(0.16)]/2 = (1 +/- 0.4)/2, so z' = 0.3 and z'' = 0.7. The tipping point is the SMALLER root z' = 0.3; the platform must get more than 30% of users on board.
why_wrong: 0.21 is the price, not a root.
0.50 is where the curve peaks (p = 1/4), not the tipping point.
0.70 is the large stable root z'', not the tipping point.

mcq.q: Same model (p* = z(1 - z)). If the price is p* = 0.24, what are the two non-zero equilibria?
mcq.explanation: sqrt(1 - 4 x 0.24) = sqrt(0.04) = 0.2, so z = (1 +/- 0.2)/2 = 0.4 and 0.6. A price close to the peak of 1/4 squeezes the two roots together near 1/2: the tipping point is high and the final market is small.
why_wrong: Uses p and 1 - p instead of solving the quadratic.
0.1 and 0.9 are the roots for p = 0.09.
0.2 and 0.8 are the roots for p = 0.16.

mcq.q: Same model (p* = z(1 - z)). The platform sets p* = 0.30. What happens?
options: Two equilibria, z' = 0.3 and z'' = 0.7
Only z = 0 is an equilibrium: the product dies
One equilibrium at z = 0.5
Only z = 0.7 is an equilibrium
mcq.explanation: z(1 - z) has a maximum of 1/4 = 0.25 at z = 1/2. Since 0.30 > 0.25, 1 - 4p = -0.2 < 0 and there is no real root. No positive fraction of users would pay 0.30, so only z = 0 remains.
why_wrong: 0.3 and 0.7 are the roots for p = 0.21; here p is above the peak.
z = 0.5 is the single tangent root only when p is exactly 0.25.
No positive root exists when p > 1/4.

mcq.q: With p* = 0.16 (equilibria 0, 0.2, 0.8), a new platform launches and reaches only 15% of the market. If nothing else changes, where does the market end up?
options: Falls to z = 0, because 15% is below the tipping point of 20%
Grows to z = 0.8, because any start above zero grows
Stays at 15%, because every point is an equilibrium
Grows to z = 0.2 and stays there, because 0.2 is stable
mcq.explanation: Below z' = 0.2, the value r(z)f(z) = 0.15 x 0.85 = 0.1275 is less than the price 0.16, so users leave and demand falls to 0. Only between 0.2 and 0.8 do users keep joining until the stable point z'' = 0.8. This is why z' is unstable and called the tipping point.
why_wrong: Users join only above z' = 0.2, not from any positive start.
Only 0, 0.2 and 0.8 are equilibria; 0.15 is not one.
0.2 is UNSTABLE; small moves away from it grow or shrink.

mcq.q: A platform cuts its introductory price from p* = 0.16 to p* = 0.09 (model p* = z(1 - z)). What happens to z' and z''?
options: z' moves right to 0.3; z'' moves left to 0.7
Both z' and z'' move right, to 0.3 and 0.9
z' stays at 0.2; only z'' moves to 0.9
z' moves left to 0.1; z'' moves right to 0.9
mcq.explanation: At p = 0.09, sqrt(1 - 0.36) = 0.8, so z = (1 +/- 0.8)/2 = 0.1 and 0.9. Lowering the price gives two wins: the tipping point falls from 0.2 to 0.1 (easier to reach) and the stable market grows from 0.8 to 0.9. This is why platforms use free trials and low introductory prices.
why_wrong: That is what happens when the price RISES (to 0.21).
z' moves left, not right, when the price falls.
Both roots change when the price changes.

mcq.q: Group 1's Week 8 critique of the network-effects matrix (same-side on one axis, cross-side on the other) judged the 'data networks' circle (Netflix, Google, Yelp, Waze) as 'low / low'. What was the group's verdict?
options: Fully correct, because all data networks only learn from usage data
Partly wrong: Google and Yelp have high cross-side effects and Waze has high same-side effects
Wrong only for Netflix, which has strong cross-side effects
Correct, but the circle should move to 'high / high' with iOS and Xbox
mcq.explanation: The group found the data-networks placement partly wrong: Google and Yelp link users with advertisers or businesses (high cross-side), and Waze gets better as more drivers report traffic (high same-side). Netflix fits, since it has only a data effect. Takeaway: placement depends on which users and which effect you measure.
why_wrong: The group said the circle was only partly right, not fully correct.
Netflix was the one that DID fit the 'low / low' placement.
The group did not move the whole circle to high/high; it said each member differs.

mcq.q: SideCar (2011) had good technology but poor marketing. Too few drivers joined, riders faced long waits and left. In network-effects terms, SideCar failed because it:
options: Set a price above 1/4, so only z = 0 existed
Charged drivers a 25% cut, so good drivers left
Never got past the tipping point z' (never reached critical mass)
Reached the stable point z'' but then faced quality problems
mcq.explanation: SideCar never built enough users on both sides to pass the tipping point, so the market slid back towards zero. Lesson 1: achieving the network effect is vital (market heavily, incentivise the supply side, low fees, easy sign-up).
why_wrong: The lecture does not say SideCar's price was the issue; the problem was too few users.
The 25% cut is the Homejoy story, not SideCar.
SideCar never reached a large stable user base.

mcq.q: Homejoy took a 25% cut, experienced cleaners left, and customers who found a good cleaner then booked them directly outside the app. Which lesson from the lecture does this mainly illustrate?
options: Know your market: providers' reactions and customers bypassing the platform
Lower information search costs with filters and ratings
Platforms in data networks need only same-side effects
Lower the price to move z' to the right
mcq.explanation: Homejoy misjudged how providers would react to its fee and how easily customers could bypass it (disintermediation) and switch. That is Lesson 2, know your market; the fall in cleaning quality also links to Lesson 3, quality control.
why_wrong: Lowering search costs is a platform 'invention' (Yelp), not the lesson from Homejoy.
This is about the matrix and does not explain Homejoy's failure.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's slide shows two pictures. In picture 1, value flows one way: producer → firm → consumer. In picture 2, the firm sits in the middle while outside producers and consumers create value with each other. Which statement is correct?

Picture 2 is a pipe, because value passes through the firm
Both are platforms; picture 2 simply has more users
Picture 2 is a platform: its role is enabling value-creating interactions between external producers and consumers
mcq.explanation: A pipe makes and pushes value in one direction (picture 1). A platform orchestrates a network: its role is enabling value-creating interactions between external producers and consumers (picture 2).
why_wrong: One-way flow controlled by the firm is a pipe, not a platform.
In picture 2 value is created between outside users, which is a platform.
Picture 1 is a pipe; the difference is the direction of value, not user numbers.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's one-sided network picture shows 2 phones = 1 link, 5 phones = 10 links and 12 phones = 66 links. Using the same rule, how many links do 8 phones make?
why_wrong: 16 is 2 × 8; links grow faster than the number of phones.
56 is n(n − 1) without dividing by 2, so each link is counted twice.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's YouTube diagram has arrows between viewers and creators, plus arrows within the viewer side. A viewer shares a video with friends who are also viewers, and they all enjoy the platform more. Which effect is this?

A positive cross-side effect
A negative same-side effect
A negative cross-side effect
mcq.explanation: Viewers gaining from other viewers is a same-side effect, and it is positive because they enjoy the platform more. Cross-side would be viewers gaining from more creators (or creators from more viewers).
why_wrong: Cross-side links two DIFFERENT groups (viewers ↔ creators); here both are viewers.
Negative same-side is like eBay sellers competing; here viewers benefit.

mcq.q: Prof Lim's stability chart for p* = z(1 − z) has arrows: below z′ they point left toward 0; between z′ and z″ they point right toward z″; above z″ they point left back to z″. What do the arrows tell you?
options: z′ and z″ are both stable, and 0 is unstable
z′ is stable, z″ is unstable, and 0 is never reached
0 and z″ are stable; z′ is unstable, the tipping point the firm must get past
Only z′ is an equilibrium; 0 and z″ are just ends of the curve
mcq.explanation: Arrows point AWAY from z′ (left to 0, right to z″), so z′ is unstable: the tipping point or critical mass. Arrows point TOWARD 0 and z″, so both are stable.
why_wrong: Arrows move away from z′, so it cannot be stable; 0 attracts the market from below z′.
It is the reverse: z″ attracts the market, z′ repels it, and 0 is reached from below z′.
0, z′ and z″ are all equilibria where p* = r(z)f(z).

mcq.q: Which statement best captures the difference between omnichannel and multichannel retailing?
options: Omnichannel means selling only online; multichannel means selling online and in stores
Omnichannel means having more channels than multichannel
Omnichannel is for groceries; multichannel is for fashion
Omnichannel integrates all channels into one seamless experience; multichannel runs channels as separate silos
mcq.explanation: Omnichannel is an integrated sales approach that blends store advantages with information-rich online shopping, giving a seamless experience on desktop, mobile, phone or in store. Multichannel can have the same channels but runs them as separate silos.
why_wrong: Omnichannel includes stores; it is not online only.
The number of channels is not the point; integration is.

mcq.q: Which of these is listed in the lecture as an advantage of shopping in a STORE rather than online?

Help with setup and repair
Extensive reviews and recommendations
Broad, easy-to-search selection

Reviews and recommendations are an online advantage.

mcq.q: The information-fulfilment matrix (Bell, Gallino & Moreno 2014) classifies retail models using which two dimensions?
options: How the customer gets product information (offline/online) and how the order is fulfilled (pickup/delivery)
Where the sale is paid (online/offline) and who owns the stock (retailer/supplier)
Product type (standard/experiential) and price level (low/high)
Customer type (B2B/B2C) and channel count (single/many)
mcq.explanation: The axes are information (offline or online: where the customer learns about the product) and fulfilment (pickup or delivery). This gives Q1 B&M, Q2 online-and-offline, Q3 offline-and-online and Q4 pure-play.
why_wrong: A common trap: the matrix is not about where the sale is made or who owns stock.
Product type decides which quadrant fits best, but it is not an axis.
Customer type and channel count are not the matrix axes.

mcq.q: A shopper orders a phone charger on a retailer's app at lunch and collects it from the retailer's store on the way home. Which quadrant is this?
options: Q1: traditional brick-and-mortar
Q3: offline-and-online
Q2: online-and-offline (buy online, pick up in store)
Q4: pure-play e-commerce
mcq.explanation: The customer gets information and orders online, and the order is fulfilled by pickup. Online information + pickup is Q2, which includes BOPIS (buy online, pick up or return in store).
why_wrong: Q1 uses offline information; here the shopper used the app.
Q3 is offline information + delivery; here there is no delivery.
Q4 is online information + home delivery; here the shopper picks up.

mcq.q: A customer tries on running shoes in a store, then goes home and orders them online to be delivered. This 'showrooming' falls in which quadrant?
options: Q1: offline information, pickup
Q2: online information, pickup
Q3: offline information, delivery
Q4: online information, delivery
mcq.explanation: The customer learns about the product offline (in the store) and receives it by delivery. Offline information + delivery is Q3, offline-and-online, which includes showrooming and 'buy in store, deliver home'.
why_wrong: Q1 means the customer carries the goods home from the store; here they are delivered.
Q2 is online information + pickup, e.g., BOPIS, the opposite case.
Q4 means information also comes from online; here it came from the store visit.

mcq.q: A shopper reads reviews and compares prices on her phone, then drives to a store, buys the TV and carries it home herself. Which quadrant is this?
options: Q2: online information, pickup
Q1: offline information, pickup
Q3: offline information, delivery
Q4: online information, delivery
mcq.explanation: Information came from online research, and fulfilment was pickup (she took it home herself). 'Research online, buy in store' is part of Q2, online-and-offline.
why_wrong: Q1 would mean she learned about the TV only in the store.
There is no delivery here, and her information was online.
She was not delivered the TV; she picked it up.

mcq.q: Bonobos, an online clothing brand, opens 'guideshops' where customers try on clothes; the shops hold no stock to take away, and orders are shipped home. In the matrix, this is a strategic move from:
options: Q1 to Q2
Q2 to Q1
Q3 to Q4
Q4 to Q3
mcq.explanation: Bonobos started as pure-play e-commerce (Q4). Adding showrooms gives customers offline information while keeping home delivery, which is Q3. The two strategic moves in the lecture are Q1 to Q2 (stores add online information) and Q4 to Q3 (pure-plays add showrooms).
why_wrong: Q1 to Q2 is a store retailer adding online information, e.g., an app showing stock.
Q2 to Q1 would remove online information, which is not a strategy in the lecture.
This reverses the direction; Bonobos is adding showrooms, not removing them.

mcq.q: In Group 1's Q2 vs Q3 analysis, which is a main RETAILER benefit of Q2 (store as a collection point)?
options: Less stock and floor space needed in each store
Lower last-mile cost plus extra foot traffic and add-on sales
Full control over home delivery and installation
Staff demos that lift conversion for bulky goods
mcq.explanation: In Q2 the customer does the last mile, so the retailer saves delivery cost, and pickups bring people into the store who often buy more (62% of Walmart pickup shoppers bought extra items). Stores also act as mini fulfilment centres.
why_wrong: Less stock and floor space is a Q3 (showroom) benefit.
Controlling delivery and installation is a Q3 benefit.
Demos for bulky goods are a Q3 showroom benefit.

mcq.q: According to Group 1's analysis, which product is the best fit for a Q3 (store as showroom, deliver home) model?
options: A sofa that customers want to sit on before buying
A weekly basket of standard groceries
A familiar phone accessory bought many times
A pack of printer paper
mcq.explanation: Q3 fits high-value, bulky, experiential goods (furniture, cars, mattresses): customers want to try them, and they are hard to carry, so delivery and installation help. Q3 optimises experience and certainty.
why_wrong: Standard groceries fit Q2: familiar goods, quick pickup.
Familiar accessories fit Q2; there is no need to try them first.
Printer paper is a standard good that needs no try-out, so Q2 or Q4 fits better.

mcq.q: Group 1 noted a key weakness of the Q3 (showroom) model for a retailer. What is it?
options: Customers must pay a delivery fee for groceries
In-store picking of online orders is costly
Customers live too far from collection points
Showrooming leakage: shoppers try in store but buy from a rival online
mcq.explanation: In Q3, customers can learn in the store and then buy elsewhere online (the group cited 57% leakage). Delivery of bulky goods is also costly. Q2's weaknesses are different: in-store picking cost and customers far from stores.
why_wrong: Grocery delivery fees are not the Q3 weakness in the group's table.
In-store picking cost is a Q2 weakness.
Distance to collection points is a Q2 weakness.

mcq.q: Among the ways brick-and-mortar retailers can fight back, which metric does the lecture say they should move away from?

Same-store sales
Online conversion rate
Customer satisfaction
mcq.explanation: Same-store sales ignore sales that a store helps create online (e.g., research in store, order online). Retailers should move away from it and judge by ROIC and growth, as Rigby shows with Amazon.
why_wrong: ROIC is the measure Rigby recommends using, not dropping.
Conversion is not the metric the lecture says to drop.
Satisfaction is not named as a metric to abandon.

mcq.q: Tesco Homeplus put pictures of products with QR codes on subway station walls in Seoul, and shoppers scanned them to order for home delivery. What result does the lecture report?

Online sales fell as customers preferred stores
Over 10,000 users in 3 months and online sales up 130%
Delivery cost fell by 28%
mcq.explanation: The Homeplus 'virtual store' gained more than 10,000 users in 3 months and online sales rose 130%. It is an example of a retailer integrating retail and logistics by bringing ordering to where shoppers wait.
why_wrong: The lecture does not report store visits doubling.
Online sales rose, not fell.
28% is the last-mile share of delivery cost (T7), not a Tesco result.

mcq.q: Which company path matches the lecture's example of 'e-commerce moving into logistics and then into physical stores'?
options: Amazon: online store, then FBA logistics, then Amazon Go stores
SF Express: logistics, then stores with no stock
Tesco: stores, then subway QR ordering
Bonobos: online store, then guideshops
mcq.explanation: Amazon began in e-commerce, built logistics (Fulfilment by Amazon), then opened stores (Amazon Go). It is one of the firms (with Alibaba and JD) heading towards the 'grand integration' of e-commerce, logistics, B&M retail, cloud, e-payment and AI.

Tesco went from stores to online ordering, the opposite direction.
Bonobos added showrooms but did not build logistics for others.

mcq.q: Rigby (2011) notes Amazon's operating margin was only about 4% versus about 6% for traditional retailers, yet its 5-year ROI was 17% versus 6.5%. What lesson does he draw?
options: Amazon was less healthy because its margin was lower
Traditional retailers should cut prices to match Amazon's margin
Judge retailers by return on invested capital and growth, not by margin
Margin and ROI always move together, so the data must be wrong
mcq.explanation: Amazon used its capital far more efficiently (no stores, so far less capital tied up), so its ROIC was more than double even with a thinner margin, and its market value matched many big chains combined. The lesson: value comes from ROIC and growth, not margin.
why_wrong: A lower margin did not mean weaker; ROI was much higher.
Cutting prices alone would lower their margin without fixing capital efficiency.
Margin and ROI can differ when capital use differs, so there is no error.

options: Stores cannibalise online sales, so retailers should close them
Physical stores lift online sales nearby: the channels complement each other
Online shoppers avoid areas with many stores
The online share depends only on delivery speed
mcq.explanation: Having a store nearby raised the retailer's share of online sales, so stores and online support each other. This is the core omnichannel message: online and offline complement each other to raise revenue, cut cost and improve service.
why_wrong: The data show the opposite: online share is HIGHER near stores.
Online share was higher, not lower, near stores.
The comparison is about store presence, not delivery speed.

mcq.q: Discussion (slide 4): a store is out of a book, so staff use an in-store kiosk to order it shipped to the shopper's home. In the information-fulfilment matrix, where does this sit?

Q2: online information with in-store pickup (BOPIS)
Q1: traditional B&M, learn in store and carry home
Q4: pure-play e-commerce, learn online and delivered home

The shopper does not carry the item home; it is delivered.

A Q1 store; SF is copying traditional supermarkets to fill its trucks
A Q3 store; a logistics firm moving into retail to fill its network, own customer data and avoid being squeezed by JD and Cainiao
A Q4 store; SF is turning into a pure-play website with a showroom

Shoppers do not carry goods home; items are delivered (not Q1).

E-payment
AI and autonomous technology
Contract manufacturing
