mcq.q: Prof Lim's course overview groups the topics by the outcome they target. Which topics sit under 'Cost ↓'?
options: Online retailing, marketplaces, and analytics & AI
Supply chain, order fulfilment, and last-mile delivery
Service platforms and omnichannel
Analytics & AI, service platforms, and last-mile delivery
mcq.explanation: The overview groups topics as: revenue ↑ (online retailing, marketplaces, analytics & AI), cost ↓ (supply chain, order fulfilment, last mile) and service level ↑ (platforms, omnichannel).
why_wrong: These are the 'Revenue ↑' topics.
These are the 'Service level ↑' topics.
This mixes one topic from each group.

saq.q: Explain FOUR advantages and THREE disadvantages of online retailing compared with brick-and-mortar retailing. Which disadvantage does the course see as the biggest, and why?
model_answer: No stores: saves rent, staff and utilities; stock is pooled in a few DCs, so less safety stock is needed (less inventory, not zero).
Attractive cash conversion cycle: high inventory turns mean Amazon is paid 19 days before it pays suppliers (−19 days vs +78 for a typical book retailer).
Demand data, not just sales data: click-stream shows what customers view together, which supports personalised assortment, promotions and prices.
Flexible fulfilment: any FC can serve any zone, improving service (though outbound cost can rise).

Disadvantages: fulfilment cost (manual picking, the most costly step, plus last mile); technology cost, which never stops (class answer: a VARIABLE cost, because it grows with suppliers, updates and security); more exposed to seasonal peaks because orders are picked after they arrive (like make-to-order).

Biggest: fulfilment + shipping cost, because going online moves the cost from stores into picking and delivering every single order. This is why the rest of the course (supply chain, equipment, picking, last mile) focuses on cutting it.
marking: 2 marks: four correct advantages, each briefly explained (0.5 each)
1.5 marks: three correct disadvantages, each explained (0.5 each)
1 mark: names fulfilment + shipping cost as the biggest
0.5 mark: explains WHY (cost moves from stores to each-order picking and delivery)
mistakes: Saying online retailers need no inventory (they hold less, pooled).
Listing 'flexible fulfilment' as a disadvantage, confusing it with fulfilment cost.
Saying online is less affected by seasonal peaks (it is more affected).

saq.q: Amazon's cash conversion cycle is −19 days while a typical book retailer's is +78 days. Explain what these numbers mean, why Amazon's is negative, and why this matters for growth.
model_answer: The cash conversion cycle is the time between paying suppliers and receiving cash from customers (inventory days + receivable days − payable days).
−19 days: Amazon collects from customers 19 days BEFORE it pays suppliers; +78 days: the book retailer pays suppliers 78 days before customers pay. The gap is 97 days.
Amazon's is negative because of high inventory turns (about 14× a year vs ~2.5× for B&N), a 'sell all, carry few' model with drop-shipping, and instant card payment from customers.
This means suppliers' money funds Amazon's operations: it needs little working capital and can grow fast without heavy borrowing.
A store retailer must fund its shelf stock for months, which ties up cash and limits growth.
marking: 1 mark: correct meaning of CCC
1 mark: correct reading of −19 and +78 (who pays first)
1 mark: reason for negative CCC (turns, drop-ship, quick payment)
1 mark: why it matters (free financing, growth)
mistakes: Mixing up the sign: thinking −19 means Amazon pays suppliers first.
Computing the gap as 59 days instead of 97.
Confusing a good cash cycle with a high profit margin.

saq.q: Barnes & Noble is considering fully integrating its online business with its 793 stores. Discuss the advantages of integration and the operational challenges it would face.
model_answer: Advantage (revenue): order in store when a title is out of stock, so the sale is saved instead of lost.
Advantage (cost): buy online, pick up in store removes last-mile delivery cost and brings foot traffic and add-on sales.
Advantage (cost/service): pooled inventory and shared customer data across channels; easy returns in store; one brand experience.
Challenge: legacy systems that cannot see store stock in real time, so online promises may be wrong.
Challenge: different picking (single units for online vs cartons for stores) needs new processes and equipment; staff need training.
Challenge: channel conflict and incentives (who gets credit for a sale), plus tax/legal structure (BN.com was a separate company to avoid sales tax) and keeping prices consistent.
Conclusion: integration is worth it (B&N did take BN.com back in 2003 and added kiosks and BOPIS) but only if IT and incentives are fixed first.
marking: 3 marks: three advantages, ideally framed as revenue, cost and service
3 marks: three operational challenges, each explained (full marks only if linked to case facts)
mistakes: Listing only general benefits with no operational challenges.
Forgetting incentives / channel conflict, which is a key barrier.
Not using any case facts (793 stores, separate BN.com, legacy systems).
saq.source: slides01 in-class Q / Ch 1 Problems / Wharton case

saq.q: Using the Online Book Retailing case, explain why Amazon succeeded online while Barnes & Noble's BN.com struggled.
model_answer: Amazon's model was 'sell all, carry few': 1M+ titles listed but only ~2,000 stocked in 1995; the rest drop-shipped or ordered from wholesaler Ingram.
Amazon invested heavily in the back end: 80% of IT spend on back-office logistics; inventory turned ~14× a year (11–21) vs ~2.3–2.8 at B&N.
This gave a negative cash cycle (−19 days) and low return rates (1–2%).
B&N set BN.com up as a separate company to avoid sales tax; it stocked 600k–750k titles with inflexible legacy systems and was never profitable.
Lesson: a strong store brand does not transfer online by itself; logistics and IT are 'the iceberg below the waterline'.
Caveat: Amazon also hit problems when expanding warehouses (split shipments, more inventory, IT coordination; closed McDonough in 2001), so logistics must be managed carefully.
marking: 2 marks: Amazon's model and back-end focus with facts
1 mark: performance gap (turns / cash cycle)
1 mark: B&N's weaknesses (separate company, legacy IT, slow turns)
1 mark: the lesson (brand does not transfer; logistics is the iceberg)
mistakes: Saying Amazon won because of its brand or advertising alone.
Claiming Amazon held no inventory.
Mixing up Borders (outsourced to Amazon) with B&N.

saq.q: Why would a large online retailer such as Amazon open its website to third-party sellers? And why does it prefer those sellers to use Fulfilment by Amazon rather than Sell on Amazon?
model_answer: Reason 1, one-stop shopping: the marketplace covers the long tail (slow movers, new items) without the retailer owning that stock.
Reason 2, test new products: watch which third-party items sell, then sell the winners itself.
Reason 3, learn from data: seller, product, transaction and location data help it adapt its business model.
FBA preference, 'firms that control logistics win': (a) it owns all the detailed data (demand, behaviour, delivery time);
(b) it protects its brand by controlling service quality; (c) sellers find it harder to leave (lock-in).
Extra: fee income and scale economies in its own warehouses; Prime eligibility makes the whole platform more attractive.
marking: 3 marks: three reasons to run a marketplace (1 each)
2 marks: at least two reasons for preferring FBA, explained
mistakes: Giving seller benefits (traffic, reputation) instead of the operator's reasons.
Saying FBA saves the operator warehouse investment (it needs more).
Forgetting the long-tail idea.

saq.q: 'Fulfilment by Amazon is always better for the seller than Sell on Amazon.' Do you agree? Discuss.
model_answer: Disagree: for Amazon FBA is better, but for the seller it depends on the product and its own logistics ability.
FBA benefits: Prime badge and buy-box advantage, professional logistics, less work, Amazon's shipping discounts.
FBA costs: storage fees, loss of customer data and control, lock-in (harder to leave), commingling risk.
SoA benefits: seller stays independent, keeps control and data, can sell on other channels too, and can leave easily.
SoA suits bulky, slow, high-margin or customised goods, and sellers with their own logistics or a multi-channel plan.
FBA suits small, fast-moving, standard goods where Prime speed drives sales.
Conclusion: choose by product type and capability; some sellers use both (FBA for fast movers, SoA for the rest).
marking: 1 mark: clear position ('it depends')
2 marks: FBA pros and cons for the seller
1 mark: SoA pros
2 marks: when each one wins, with product examples
mistakes: Answering from Amazon's view only.
One-sided answer with no conditions.
Mixing up which model makes the seller ship.

saq.q: Explain how a consignment contract with revenue sharing works on an online marketplace and why the operator likes it. A seller consigns goods priced at $50 with r = 0.2 and sells 300 units: how much does each party receive?
model_answer: Under consignment the manufacturer/seller keeps ownership of the stock in the retailer's warehouse until a unit is sold.
For each unit sold the retailer keeps r·p and the manufacturer gets (1 − r)·p.
Calculation: retailer = 0.2 × $50 × 300 = $3,000; manufacturer = 0.8 × $50 × 300 = $12,000 (total sales $15,000). Unsold units earn nothing and are the seller's problem.
Why the operator likes it: (i) no overstock risk; (ii) no need to negotiate price or quantity with each of thousands of sellers;
(iii) every online sale is tracked, so the revenue split is automatic and easy to enforce.
Prof Lim's model adds a storage fee s per unit of volume to ration limited space.
marking: 1 mark: ownership stays with manufacturer
1 mark: r·p / (1 − r)·p split
1 mark: correct numbers $3,000 and $12,000
2 marks: two or three reasons the operator likes it
mistakes: Swapping r and (1 − r).
Paying on units shipped instead of units sold.
Saying the retailer bears overstock risk.
saq.source: slides02 / Ch 2 / Lim, Wang & Wu (2015) / F4

saq.q: Describe the structure of Prof Lim's consignment model (Lim, Wang & Wu 2015) and state its main managerial results.
model_answer: Stackelberg game: the retailer is the leader and sets the revenue share r and storage fee s (charged per unit of volume); each manufacturer is a follower and sets its price pᵢ and quantity qᵢ.
Constraint: shared warehouse capacity Σqᵢvᵢ ≤ V; demand is random and price-sensitive, Dᵢ = aᵢpᵢ^(−bᵢ)εᵢ. Solved backwards.
Costs: manufacturer Mᵢ = mᵢ + s·vᵢ, retailer Rᵢ = dᵢ − s·vᵢ; the fee shifts cost between them.
Result 1: if manufacturing costs are similar, s = 0 is enough (revenue share alone).
Result 2: if costs differ a lot, set s > 0 so bulky cheap items (diapers) do not crowd out valuable ones (diamonds).
Result 3: expanding capacity V can benefit both the retailer and the manufacturers.
marking: 1 mark: leader/follower roles and decisions
1 mark: capacity constraint / backward solution
2 marks: two of the three results
mistakes: Making the manufacturer the leader.
Saying s is charged per unit sold.
Saying capacity expansion hurts sellers.

saq.q: Demand for a new style is estimated as Y = 70.50719 − 0.60658X, where X is price. Unit cost is 75. The price must not exceed the competitor's price of 134.99, the margin on cost must be at least 50%, and X ≥ 5. Find the revenue-maximising price and explain which constraint is binding.
model_answer: Margin constraint: (X − 75)/75 ≥ 0.5 → X ≥ 112.5. Feasible range: 112.5 ≤ X ≤ 134.99.
58.12 is not feasible. Since R is a downward parabola that falls for all X > 58.12, the best feasible price is the lowest allowed: X* = 112.5.
The 50% margin floor is binding; the competitor cap (134.99) is not binding. Business meaning: the firm accepts lower revenue to protect its margin.
marking: 1 mark: revenue function
1 mark: X⁰ = 58.12
1 mark: margin floor X ≥ 112.5
2 marks: X* = 112.5 with reason (R falls after 58.12)
1 mark: names binding vs non-binding constraint
mistakes: Giving 58.12 as the final answer without checking constraints.
Choosing 134.99 because 'higher price = more revenue'.
Using margin on price ((X − 75)/X), which gives X ≥ 150.

saq.q: 'Pricing fashion is an art, not a science.' Using the Flashion case, discuss whether analytics can be used to price first-exposure styles.
model_answer: Art side: trends are hard to quantify; little data on competitors' prices; colour, style and quality are hard to measure; value differs by person.

Science side: e-commerce data is rich (click-stream, traffic); some metrics are clear (price, discount, category); clear success measure (large demand); one wrong prediction has small impact across thousands of styles.
Method: learn demand drivers from past first-exposure styles (30,389 styles in the data; higher discount → higher sell-through), predict demand for new styles, then optimise price within constraints.
Limits: sold-out styles hide true demand (censored, lost sales are missing data); feature choice is still art.
Conclusion: combine both. The model forecasts and suggests a price; the buyer adds judgement and signs off. Win sceptics like Priscilla Johnson with a pilot or A/B test.
marking: 1 mark: art arguments
1 mark: science arguments
1 mark: how the model works (forecast then optimise)
1 mark: a limitation (censored demand / feature choice)
1 mark: balanced conclusion with implementation step
mistakes: Taking a one-sided view.
Saying new styles cannot be forecast because they have no history.
Treating the 80% sell-through target as the true objective.

saq.q: Classify the data a flash-sale retailer would use to predict demand into available, derived and missing data. Why does the missing data matter?
model_answer: Available: price, MSRP, event timing (month/day/time), competitors' prices, quantity sold.
Derived: discount = (MSRP − price)/MSRP, number of styles in the event, relative price, weekend/weekday.
Missing: lost sales (time of stock-out, site traffic).

Why it matters: when a style sells out, sales are capped at inventory, so true demand is hidden (censored). A model trained on sales will under-state demand for popular styles and may push prices too low.
Fix ideas: record stock-out time and traffic, or treat sold-out styles as 'demand at least equal to stock'.
marking: 1 mark: available data
1 mark: derived data
1 mark: missing data = lost sales
1 mark: censored-demand consequence
mistakes: Calling lost sales 'derived'.
Calling discount 'available' rather than derived.
Not explaining the bias from sold-out styles.

saq.q: Compare rule-based AI with neural networks (deep learning). Explain why 'if AI is the electricity, data is the oil'.
model_answer: Rule-based AI: humans write if-then rules (e.g., 'black-and-white patches → panda'). Easy to understand and fine for simple problems, but it breaks down as complexity grows.
Neural networks: layers of artificial neurons learn patterns from lots of labelled examples ('panda / no panda'); they need data and computing power.
Uses: face recognition, speech, translation, card fraud, insurance approval, consumer prediction, robot navigation, driving.
More data makes AI smarter: average engineers with lots of data beat top experts with little data.
So data powers AI the way oil powered industry; firms with more data (e.g., large online platforms) gain an advantage, and data becomes a natural resource.
marking: 1 mark: rule-based explained with its limit
1 mark: neural network explained with its needs
1 mark: 'more data beats experts' point
1 mark: meaning of the slogan
mistakes: Saying rule-based needs more data.
Saying deep learning needs little data.
Not linking the slogan to data as a competitive resource.

saq.q: Name the three key decisions in aggregate supply chain planning for an online retailer. For each, state whether it is push or pull and explain why the three should be decided jointly.
model_answer: Replenishment: when and how much to order from each supplier; balances fixed ordering cost against holding cost. Push (made before demand is known).
Allocation: how much of each product to store in each warehouse (FC), to keep stock close to its demand. Push (anticipative).
Fulfilment: which warehouse retrieves and ships each order, to minimise shipping cost once demand is known. Pull (reactive).
Online retailers have fulfilment flexibility: any FC with stock can serve a zone.
So allocation affects which FC ships each order, and that affects what to order from suppliers; the decisions depend on each other.
Deciding them separately gives a higher total cost, which is why Prof Lim's JRAF model optimises all three together.
marking: 1 mark each: correctly names and explains replenishment, allocation, fulfilment (max 3)
1 mark: correct push (replenishment, allocation) vs pull (fulfilment) split
1 mark: explains that fulfilment flexibility makes the decisions interdependent, so joint planning lowers total cost
mistakes: Calling allocation a pull decision (it is push)
Listing the decisions without saying why they must be joint
Mixing up allocation (stock in each FC) with fulfilment (which FC ships)

saq.q: Compare the demand that a brick-and-mortar retailer's warehouses serve with the demand an online retailer's warehouses serve. What does this difference mean for supply chain planning?
model_answer: B&M: few orders per day, each for a large quantity, shipped to the retailer's own stores.
B&M: no fulfilment flexibility; if one warehouse is out of stock, the stores cannot get it from another warehouse.
Online: many orders per day, each for a small quantity, shipped to homes.
Online: fulfilment flexibility; any FC holding the item can serve the zone.
Implication: flexibility raises service level but can raise outbound shipping cost and makes allocation and replenishment harder to plan.
So the online retailer needs joint planning (JRAF), and picking many small orders becomes a key bottleneck (T6).
marking: 1 mark: B&M few, large orders
1 mark: online many, small orders
1 mark: fulfilment flexibility (online has it, B&M does not)
1 mark: implication for planning (service vs shipping cost, joint planning)
mistakes: Saying B&M has fulfilment flexibility
Saying flexibility always cuts cost (it can raise shipping cost)

saq.q: Describe the joint replenishment-allocation-fulfilment (JRAF) model: its objective, its main constraints, and how it guarantees a feasible solution.
model_answer: Decision variables: replenishment (how much to order), allocation (how much to send to each FC), fulfilment (which FC ships to which zone) and inventory levels.
Objective: minimise total cost = production (fixed setup + variable) + holding at FCs + allocation + fulfilment costs.
Constraints: supplier production capacity; everything received is allocated; warehouse capacity; demand fully met (no backlog or lost sales).
Flow balance: next period's inventory = current inventory + allocated − shipped.
Feasibility: drop-shipping from the supplier is added as an extra, expensive warehouse 'FC J+1', so demand can always be met.
Solved with off-the-shelf optimisation software; a robust-optimisation version handles uncertain demand.
marking: 2 marks: objective with all four cost terms (1 mark for at least two)
2 marks: at least four of the five constraint types
1 mark: drop-shipping as FC J+1 keeps it feasible
1 mark: mentions robust version for uncertain demand or solving with software
mistakes: Adding a stockout penalty to the objective (demand must be fully met)
Forgetting the flow balance constraint
Saying drop-shipping is cheap (it is the expensive backup)

saq.q: Using the Forbes (2016) reading, explain why Amazon and Alibaba are investing heavily in their own logistics, and give one trade-off of doing so.
model_answer: Delivery systems date from the 19th century and are slow and costly; carriers limit speed and service.
Amazon doubled its leased cargo-jet fleet and shipped 1 billion of its own parcels in a year; it was forecast to out-ship FedEx by 2019.
Alibaba's Cainiao planned a $16B investment: about 1,800 DCs and 97,000 delivery stations in 600+ cities.
Lesson: logistics becomes the critical success factor, so retailers integrate vertically (speed, cost control, capacity, data).
Trade-off: very large fixed capital and risk, in exchange for control over speed and service instead of relying on carriers.
marking: 1 mark: reason (speed/cost/control of slow carrier networks)
1 mark: correct Amazon example
1 mark: correct Cainiao example
1 mark: trade-off (fixed capital vs control)
mistakes: Attributing the $16B to Amazon (it is Cainiao)
Saying Amazon had already overtaken FedEx (it was a 2019 forecast)
saq.source: Forbes (2016) Amazon & Alibaba bet the future on SCM

saq.q: For each type of demand (pallet, case, piece), state suitable storage equipment and handling equipment, and give one reason for each match.
model_answer: Pallet: single-deep (selective) racks; handled by counterbalance lift trucks (one pallet at a time) or turret trucks (very narrow aisles of 5–7 ft, turret turns 90°); AS/RS and conveyors also possible.
Case: pallet flow racks (tilted, rollers; pick and restock from different aisles, so good for high-throughput SKUs).
Case handling: order-picker trucks (long travel, several cases per trip); AS/RS, conveyors, Boston Dynamics robots.
Piece, slow movers: bin-shelving (shallow; restocked at the same face, so only fine when restocking is rare).
Piece, fast movers: gravity flow racks (deep, tilted, restocked from the back; high SKU density; pick-to-light).
Piece handling: AS/RS (bin version), Kiva (moves shelf pods), AutoStore (robots fetch bins from a cube grid).
marking: 1 mark: pallet storage; 1 mark: pallet handling with a reason
1 mark: case storage; 1 mark: case handling with a reason
1 mark: piece storage split slow vs fast; 1 mark: piece handling/robots
mistakes: Putting pallet flow racks under pallet demand
Using bin-shelving for fast movers
Placing Boston Dynamics under piece picking

saq.q: Compare bin-shelving and gravity flow racks for piece picking. Which items should go on each, and why?
model_answer: Bin-shelving: shallow shelves; picking and restocking are done from the same face.
Because it holds little and restocking blocks the pick face, it suits slow movers (the long tail of SKUs).
Gravity flow racks: deep, tilted lanes with one case on the face; restocked from the back.
Restocking does not interrupt picking and SKU density is high, so they suit fast movers; often used with pick-to-light.
In a fast-pick area: gravity flow racks for popular items, bin-shelving for the long tail.
marking: 1 mark: describes bin-shelving design
1 mark: bin-shelving → slow movers with reason
1 mark: describes gravity flow rack design
1 mark: gravity flow → fast movers with reason
mistakes: Reversing the two (correct match: bin-shelving = slow movers, gravity flow = fast movers)
Saying gravity flow racks are restocked from the front

saq.q: Group 1's Week 4 exercise: give one example each of piece demand in B2B, B2C and C2C, and explain why piece demand is usually the hardest to fulfil.
model_answer: B2B piece: an MRO spare part sent to a factory. B2C piece: Amazon delivers one book. C2C piece: one used iPhone sold on Carousell.
Every unit is touched, so labour cost per unit is highest.
Pieces fit poorly with mechanisation; automating needs costly goods-to-person robots (Kiva, AutoStore).
Demand is erratic and unpooled across many SKUs, causing long travel between picks.
Downstream is costly too: each order ships as a single parcel and returns are common.
Refinement: difficulty depends on the order profile relative to the handling unit, not the channel label (Amazon is B2C but has the hardest piece-picking problem).
marking: 1 mark: three correct examples
3 marks: any three reasons piece is hardest (1 each)
1 mark: refinement about order profile vs channel label
mistakes: Giving pallet or case examples by mistake
Claiming C2C is always hardest because of the channel name

saq.q: Explain why order-picking is the main target for cost reduction in a warehouse, and name two ways equipment or technology can reduce it.
model_answer: Warehouse flow: receiving → put-away → order-picking → checking and packing → shipping.
Order-picking is about 55% of warehouse operating expense, the largest single share.
Within picking, travel takes the most time, and travel adds no value.
Way 1: put fast movers in gravity flow racks in a fast-pick area so pickers walk less.
Way 2: goods-to-person robots (Kiva moves shelf pods; AutoStore brings bins) cut walking to zero.
Other: AS/RS, conveyors or order-picker trucks matched to the handling unit.
marking: 1 mark: ~55% of operating expense
1 mark: travel is the largest part of picking time
2 marks: two suitable technologies with how they cut travel/cost
mistakes: Saying receiving or packing is the biggest cost
Naming equipment without linking it to less travel

saq.q: State the bucket brigade rule. Three pickers have speeds 2, 1 and 5 (in jobs per hour). Explain how they should be ordered, find the interval each picker covers once the line balances, and find the throughput. State the model's assumptions.
model_answer: Rule: carry your job forward until the downstream colleague takes it over (or finish at the end); then walk back and take over the upstream colleague's job (or start a new job if first).
Order slowest to fastest along the flow: speed 1, then 2, then 5. Then the line self-balances.
Throughput TH = Σv = 8 jobs per hour (sum, not average or minimum).
Assumptions: work content 1 spread evenly; constant forward speeds; instant walk-back; no passing.
marking: 1 mark: correct rule
1 mark: slowest-to-fastest order
2 marks: all three intervals correct (1 mark if two correct)
1 mark: TH = 8
1 mark: at least three assumptions
mistakes: Keeping the given order (2, 1, 5) instead of re-ordering
Giving TH as the average speed (2.67) or slowest speed (1)
Using v_i/Σv as the end point instead of the cumulative sum

saq.q: Explain why bucket brigades are better than zone picking for fast movers. List the five advantages of bucket brigades.
model_answer: Zone picking fixes each worker to a zone, so workloads are unbalanced and some workers sit idle; the path to improvement runs zone picking → cross-training → work sharing → bucket brigades.
Advantage 1: pure pull system, so WIP stays under control.
Advantage 2: workers carry jobs, so no special material-handling equipment is needed.
Advantage 3: self-balancing (with slowest-to-fastest order), so there is no need to measure task times accurately.
Advantage 4: fits the trend towards teamwork.
Advantage 5: one simple, identical rule for everyone; no management intervention needed. Used by Reader's Digest, CVS, The Gap, Subway and others.
marking: 1 mark: zone picking problem (imbalance, idle time)
4 marks: any four of the five advantages (1 mark each)
mistakes: Listing passing or buffers as advantages
Forgetting the slowest-to-fastest condition for self-balancing

saq.q: Critically assess two proposed variants of bucket brigades: (1) a blocked worker drops the job in a buffer and walks back; (2) workers circle through the line instead of walking back. Would either improve performance?
model_answer: Variant 1 (buffer): conditional yes. It removes blocking time caused by short, random delays (e.g. a one-person freezer section).
Costs of variant 1: weaker self-balancing (hand-offs no longer signal speed), more WIP and buffer space, out-of-sequence orders, extra handling.
Variant 1 does not help if downstream is systematically slower: the buffer just fills up.
Variant 2 (circling): doubtful. It removes empty walk-back (up to +25% in one simulation, Lim 2011/2012), but walk-back is a small share of time.

Circling breaks the slowest-to-fastest order: the fast worker laps and is blocked, so the line no longer self-balances and WIP rises. Only worth it with a loop/U-shaped layout, long walk-back and easy passing.
Conclusion: attack the right waste. Blocking is large and variable, so a buffer can help; walk-back is the price of self-balancing.
marking: 1 mark: variant 1 benefit
1 mark: variant 1 costs
1 mark: variant 1 condition (random vs systematic)
1 mark: variant 2 benefit and why small
1 mark: variant 2 breaks ordering/self-balancing
1 mark: clear overall verdict
mistakes: Giving a flat yes or no without conditions
Thinking walk-back is the biggest waste
Ignoring the loss of self-balancing

saq.q: Why is routing important when picking slow movers? Describe four routing heuristics and comment on how good heuristics are compared with the optimal route.
model_answer: Travel is waste and slows service; choosing the pick sequence and shortest route is a Travelling Salesman Problem. It is hard in general, but aisles make it a special case a computer can solve; in practice heuristics are used.
S-shape: go fully through every aisle with at least one pick, skip empty aisles (simplest).
Return: enter and leave each aisle with picks from the same end.
Mid-point: front half picked from the front cross-aisle, back half from the back; beats S-shape when there are few picks per aisle.
Largest gap: go in up to the largest gap and turn back; more efficient than mid-point but harder to implement. Combined: traverse or return per aisle, chosen by dynamic programming.
The best heuristic is on average about 5% worse than optimal (Petersen 1997). Robots (Kiva, AutoStore) remove walking altogether.
marking: 1 mark: travel/TSP link
3 marks: four heuristics correctly described (any three for 2 marks)
1 mark: ~5% gap to optimal
mistakes: Saying S-shape goes through empty aisles
Mixing up return and mid-point
Saying the routing problem can never be solved by a computer
saq.source: slides06 / Ch 6 / de Koster et al. (2007) / Petersen (1997)

saq.q: Using Table A from the Instacart case, compare the profit per $100 order of a conventional supermarket and Webvan. Explain why Webvan still failed and how Instacart's model avoids the same problem.
model_answer: Supermarket: 26.20 gross margin - 7.00 HQ/IT - 5.00 warehouse - 12.20 store = $2.00 per $100.
Webvan: 26.20 - 7.00 HQ/IT - 3.00 DC - 14.00 delivery = $2.20 per $100, only $0.20 better.
Webvan swapped store cost for delivery cost, but its 350,000 sq ft DCs cost about $35M each, a huge fixed cost.

The plan only worked at near-full capacity, needing about 120,000 customers within 60 miles; too few ordered (6.5% tried in Oakland), so density was too low, delivery cost per order rose and the DCs sat idle.
Instacart owns no warehouses or trucks: stores hold the stock and freelance shoppers use their own cars, so cost is variable and grows only with orders.
Instacart also uses ML to batch orders and raises prices to shift demand, but its model is easy to copy and has shopper pay disputes.
marking: 2 marks: both net profits correct with working ($2.00 and $2.20)
2 marks: Webvan failure = high fixed cost + lack of customer density (not lack of total customers)
2 marks: Instacart asset-light, variable cost, with one limitation
mistakes: Saying Webvan failed because it was less profitable per $100 (Table A shows it was slightly more profitable).
Saying Webvan lacked customers in total instead of customer density.
Forgetting the $7.00 HQ and IT charge, giving $9.20 for Webvan or $9.00 for the supermarket.

saq.q: Describe four practical challenges of last-mile delivery and, for each, name one of the five practical solutions from the lecture that helps.
model_answer: Customer not home (leave it or revisit?) - pick-up stations such as PopStation or Ninja Van lockers, or buy online, pick up in store (7-Eleven).
Hidden time for parking, finding the lift and the door, which makes timing hard to estimate - pick-up stations put many parcels in one drop.
Weather, traffic and dynamic routing (new orders mid-route) make schedules slip - Uberization gives flexible part-time capacity at peaks.
Staff turnover makes service inconsistent - autonomous vehicles give consistent service where roads and rules allow.
Maps may not exist in sparse areas - drones suit sparse, low-density areas.
Overall: VRP/VRPTW plans routes, but these real-world issues need practical solutions as well.
marking: 1 mark per challenge correctly matched to a sensible solution (max 4)
1 mark: clear link back to cost or service level (last mile up to 28% of delivery cost)
mistakes: Listing challenges with no matching solution.
Saying drones suit dense cities.
Mixing up BOPIS (pickup) with home delivery.

saq.q: 'Robots will replace human couriers in the last mile.' Critically discuss this claim.
model_answer: It depends on customer density and route complexity.
Dense + simple routes (campuses) and sparse + simple routes (drone points, road robots): robots and drones can win as their cost falls.
Complex routes (unmapped areas, lifts, gates, the 'last 50 m'): humans still win.
Humans are a variable, flexible cost that can scale up at peaks; robots are a fixed cost that needs high use, and depend on infrastructure and regulation.
So humans carry most volume this decade; a hybrid (robot to the lobby + locker) fits dense, complex zones.
The winning platform orchestrates both, e.g. DoorDash Dot robots plus Dashers, Uber Eats with Serve/Starship plus couriers.
marking: 1 mark: 'it depends' with the density x route-complexity frame
2 marks: where robots win and where humans win, with reasons
1 mark: fixed vs variable cost / regulation point
1 mark: hybrid conclusion with an example
mistakes: Taking a one-sided yes/no view.
Ignoring cost structure (fixed vs variable).
Putting drones in dense cities.

saq.q: Compare the 'go light' and 'go heavy' approaches to last-mile platforms, using Instacart and RedMart (or US and Chinese platforms) as examples. When is each better?
model_answer: Go light (US): the platform gives information and matching only; e.g., Yelp, Airbnb, Uber, and Instacart, which owns no stock, warehouses or trucks.
Go heavy (China): the platform also runs logistics; e.g., Meituan hires riders, Tujia handles cleaning and smart locks, Didi bought gas stations and workshops.
RedMart is asset-heavy too: it owns stock, a warehouse and 20 vans + 3 trucks after cross-docking and outsourced delivery failed.
Light: fast to scale, low fixed cost, but easy to copy and less control over service quality.
Heavy: more control of the customer touch point and quality, but high fixed cost that needs density and volume (Webvan's lesson).
Light suits markets with existing stores and gig labour; heavy suits dense, high-frequency markets like grocery in Singapore where service control matters.
marking: 1 mark: define go light with example
1 mark: define go heavy with example
2 marks: trade-offs (scale/cost vs control/quality)
1 mark: when each is better
mistakes: Calling China 'go light'.
Saying RedMart uses freelance shoppers.
No conclusion on when each fits.

saq.q: With network effects, consumer x will pay r(x)f(z). Let r(x) = 1 - x and f(z) = z, and the price be p* = 0.16. Find all equilibria, state which are stable, and explain what happens if the platform starts with 10% of users.
model_answer: Equilibria satisfy p* = r(z)f(z) = z(1 - z), plus z = 0, which always works because f(0) = 0.
Three equilibria: 0 (stable), z' = 0.2 (unstable, the tipping point or critical mass) and z'' = 0.8 (stable).
Below 0.2, value z(1 - z) < 0.16, so users leave and demand falls to 0; between 0.2 and 0.8, value > price, so users join until 0.8; above 0.8, users drop back to 0.8.
Starting at 10%: 0.1 x 0.9 = 0.09 < 0.16, so the platform shrinks to zero unless it pushes past 20%.
Note: the curve z(1 - z) peaks at 1/4 when z = 1/2; if p > 1/4 only z = 0 survives.
marking: 1 mark: sets up p* = z(1 - z) and includes z = 0
2 marks: correct roots 0.2 and 0.8 with working
2 marks: correct stability (0 and 0.8 stable, 0.2 unstable) with the arrow logic
1 mark: correct conclusion for the 10% start
mistakes: Calling z' stable or z'' the tipping point.
Leaving out z = 0.
Solving the no-network-effect model instead (x* = 0.84).

saq.q: Explain why platforms with network effects often charge very low introductory prices or give free trials. Contrast this with a good that has no network effect.
model_answer: Without a network effect, equilibrium solves r(x*) = p*: one equilibrium only (e.g., r = 1 - x, p = 0.16 gives x* = 0.84); a lower price just moves x* right.
With a network effect, equilibria are 0, z' (unstable tipping point) and z'' (stable), from p* = z(1 - z).
Lowering the price moves z' LEFT: the critical mass is smaller and easier to reach (p 0.16 to 0.09: z' 0.2 to 0.1).
It also moves z'' RIGHT: the final user base is bigger (0.8 to 0.9).
So early losses from low prices are repaid by later profits from a larger, stable network.
Examples: free trials, sign-up bonuses, subsidies to the supply side (drivers, hosts).
marking: 1 mark: no-network-effect case, single equilibrium
2 marks: both effects of a lower price (z' left, z'' right) with numbers
1 mark: business logic (losses now, profit later)
1 mark: relevant example
mistakes: Saying a lower price moves z' right.
Only mentioning one of the two effects.
Forgetting that above p = 1/4 the product dies.

saq.q: Critique the network-effects matrix (same-side effect on one axis, cross-side on the other). Pick one placement you agree with and one you disagree with.
model_answer: Same-side test: does a new user make the product better for users like them? Cross-side test: does it make it better for a different group?
Agree: communication networks (WhatsApp, WeChat) as high same-side / low cross-side - each friend who joins adds value to other users; but adding businesses or ads creates cross-side effects.

Disagree: data networks (Netflix, Google, Yelp, Waze) as low / low - Google and Yelp have high cross-side (users and advertisers or businesses); Waze has high same-side (more drivers, better traffic data). Only Netflix fits.
Marketplaces (Amazon, Uber, Airbnb) as high cross / low same is mostly right, but same-side effects are often negative and local (sellers compete).
Platforms/OS (iOS, Xbox) as high / high is debatable; same-side is weaker, so 'medium'.
Conclusion: placement depends on which users and which effect you measure.
marking: 1 mark: defines both axes
2 marks: one justified 'agree' with example
2 marks: one justified 'disagree' with example and better placement
mistakes: Mixing up same-side and cross-side.
Forgetting that same-side effects can be negative.
Only describing, not critiquing.

saq.q: Using SideCar and Homejoy, explain why many platforms fail, and state the three lessons from the lecture.
model_answer: SideCar: good technology, poor marketing, too few drivers, long waits, users left - it never reached critical mass (the tipping point).
Homejoy: a 25% cut drove away experienced cleaners, so quality fell; switching was easy and customers bypassed the platform once they found a good cleaner.
Wikipedia (false facts) and YouTube (inappropriate content) show quality-control problems.
Lesson 1: achieve the network effect - market heavily, incentivise the supply side, low fees, easy sign-up.
Lesson 2: know your market - competitors, provider reactions, bypassing, local market.
Lesson 3: quality control - curation and verification. Good platforms also lower search costs (Yelp ratings) and match efficiently (OkCupid).
marking: 1 mark: SideCar linked to tipping point
1 mark: Homejoy linked to fees/bypassing
3 marks: the three lessons, 1 each
mistakes: Swapping the SideCar and Homejoy stories.
Listing lessons without linking to the cases.
Saying SideCar failed because of bad technology.

saq.q: Draw and explain the information-fulfilment matrix. Give one example for each quadrant and describe the two strategic moves retailers are making.
model_answer: Axes: information (offline vs online: where the customer learns about the product) x fulfilment (pickup vs delivery).
Q1 offline information + pickup: traditional brick-and-mortar (learn in store, carry home).
Q2 online information + pickup: online-and-offline, e.g., BOPIS (Walmart pickup) or research online, buy in store.
Q3 offline information + delivery: offline-and-online, e.g., buy in store and deliver home, or showrooming (try in store, buy online), Bonobos guideshops.
Q4 online information + delivery: pure-play e-commerce.
Moves: Q1 to Q2 (stores add online information, e.g., apps showing local stock) and Q4 to Q3 (pure-plays add showrooms). Q2 and Q3 are becoming must-haves.
marking: 1 mark: correct axes
4 marks: one correct example per quadrant (1 each)
1 mark: both strategic moves
mistakes: Using online/offline SALES as the axes instead of information x fulfilment.
Putting showrooming in Q2 or BOPIS in Q3.
Forgetting to name the moves between quadrants.

saq.q: Compare Q2 (online-and-offline) and Q3 (offline-and-online) from both the retailer's and the consumer's perspective. When is each better?
model_answer: Q2 retailer: lower last-mile cost, foot traffic and add-on sales (62% of Walmart pickup shoppers bought extras), stores act as mini-FCs, easy returns.
Q2 consumer: no delivery fee, same-day pickup, online price comparison, reserved stock, return on the spot.
Q3 retailer: less stock and floor space, staff demos lift conversion, touch builds trust, controls delivery and installation.
Q3 consumer: try before buying (lower risk), expert advice, nothing to carry, installation handled.
Weaknesses: Q2 has in-store picking cost and suits customers near stores; Q3 has showrooming leakage (57%) and costly bulky delivery.

Q2 suits standard, familiar goods (groceries, accessories) and optimises convenience and cost; Q3 suits high-value, bulky, experiential goods (furniture, cars; IKEA, Bonobos) and optimises experience and certainty.
marking: 2 marks: Q2 benefits for retailer and consumer
2 marks: Q3 benefits for retailer and consumer
1 mark: one weakness each
1 mark: 'it depends' conclusion by product type
mistakes: Giving only the retailer's view.
Saying Q3 suits groceries.
No conclusion on when each wins.
saq.source: Group 1 Q2 vs Q3 submission / slides09

saq.q: Define omnichannel retailing and explain four ways brick-and-mortar retailers can fight back against pure online players.
model_answer: Omnichannel: an integrated sales approach that blends store advantages with information-rich online shopping, giving a seamless experience across desktop, mobile, phone and store (unlike multichannel silos).
People and metrics: recruit tech talent and move away from same-store sales.
Store as an asset: make it an entertaining, emotional experience (Disney, Apple, Jordan's Furniture).
Mobile and digital marketing: coupons to phones, location-based offers, apps showing reviews and local store stock (Walmart, Target, Macy's).
Channel integration: BOPIS, consistent products and prices across channels, social media dialogue.
Sell curated content (National Geographic) and offer flexible e-payment.
marking: 1 mark: correct definition with 'integrated/seamless' and contrast to multichannel
4 marks: four distinct ways with a brief reason or example (1 each)
mistakes: Defining omnichannel as simply 'many channels'.
Listing four points that are really the same idea.
No examples.

saq.q: Using Rigby (2011), explain why traditional retailers should not judge their performance by profit margin or same-store sales alone.
model_answer: Amazon's operating margin was about 4% vs 6% for traditional retailers, yet its 5-year ROI was 17% vs 6.5%.
Amazon's ROIC was more than double because it uses little capital (no stores, so far less capital tied up), so its market value matched many big chains combined.
Same-store sales miss the online sales that stores help create (stores lifted nearby online share to about 5% vs 3%; digital influences about 50% of store sales).
So judge by ROIC and growth, test and learn, and keep the digital team separate but coordinated.
marking: 2 marks: Amazon margin vs ROI numbers and the meaning
1 mark: why same-store sales mislead in an omnichannel world
1 mark: better metric (ROIC and growth)
mistakes: Saying Amazon was less profitable so less successful.
Mixing up ROI (17% vs 6.5%) with margin (4% vs 6%).

T1: Online retailers hold LESS inventory (pooled in a few DCs), not zero.
Online is MORE exposed to seasonal peaks: it works like make-to-order and cannot pre-pack.
Tech cost: class answer is VARIABLE. It never stops (suppliers, updates, tracking, security).
Cash cycle: Amazon −19 days vs book retailer +78 days. Know which way round.
T2: In the Stackelberg game the RETAILER leads (sets r and s); sellers follow.
Storage fee s is per unit of VOLUME. s = 0 if manufacturing costs are similar; s > 0 if very different.
Bigger capacity V can help BOTH retailer and sellers (win-win).
SoA: seller ships. FBA: Amazon ships. The operator prefers FBA (data, brand, lock-in).
T3: Regression finds a and b; OPTIMISATION finds the price X.
Unconstrained best 58.12 ≠ answer 112.5: the 50% margin floor binds.
Lost sales are MISSING data (censored demand), not derived data.
T4: Replenish + allocate = PUSH (before demand). Fulfil = PULL (after demand).
Online HAS fulfilment flexibility; B&M usually does not.
Drop-shipping is 'FC J+1' and keeps the JRAF model always feasible.
Bottlenecks are order-picking and the last mile.
T5: Pallet FLOW racks are for CASES, not pallets.
Bin-shelving = SLOW movers. Gravity flow = FAST movers.
Turret trucks = very narrow aisles (5–7 ft). Order-picker trucks = cases.
AS/RS can handle pallets OR pieces (bins). Boston Dynamics robots = cases.
T6: Order workers slowest → FASTEST along the flow.
Throughput = SUM of speeds, not average or minimum.
Model assumes instant walk-back and NO passing.
S-shape skips EMPTY aisles only; combined heuristic ≈ 5% off optimal.
T7: VRP depot = sortation centre, not the fulfilment centre.
'Go heavy' = China (Meituan, Tujia, Didi). 'Go light' = US.
Webvan failed from lack of DENSITY, not lack of customers.
T8: z′ is UNSTABLE (tipping point); z″ is STABLE; z = 0 is always an equilibrium.
Lower price → z′ moves LEFT and z″ moves RIGHT.
Same-side effects can be NEGATIVE (more sellers compete).
Solve z(1 − z) = p with z = [1 ± √(1 − 4p)]/2.
T9: Showrooming = try in store, buy online → Q3.
BOPIS = buy online, pick up in store → Q2.
